oances at Central High School

The War Camp Community

'Dowagers' hump" or the bump
at the base of the neck detracts
greatly from a woman's appearance.
The woman who reaches middle age
without this handicap to beauty is
unusual.


This is mainly result Of faulty
posture. Few women straighten
their spine all the way up through
the shoulders and the neck. When
you stand correctly you should not
tilt your chin up in the air. You
should keep it level, but you must
push toward the ceiling with the
top of your head. When you do
this you will be conscious Of the
back of the neck, just below the
ears.


Your muscles will feel tired when
you first begin correcting your
posture, but this will not last for
long. Think constantly OF your
posture when sitting, standing or
walking. This is the most impor-
tant factor in overcoming the ugly
bump which makes you look years
older than you are.


You also will need special exer-
cises to help correct what has al
ready happened This is good
one. Stand erect. Raise the arms
forward, shoulder width apart.
Fling the arms sideward and pull
back. This is important. When
you fling your arms sideward do not
let your head come forward. Keep
the chin level, but push back with
your neck as your arms go back
Bring arms forward again and re-
lax neck.


Massage over the fat lump will
help, too, but you must stretch the
neck and strengthen weakened
muscles, too.


The following is an easy and ef-
fective exercise for swayback, an
other of those prevalent posture
faults. Stand with your back to
the wall. Feet should be about a
foot away from the wall. Bend
the knees and place the back against
the wall. The knees should be bent
to the point where it makes it pos
sible to press the entire middle back
against the wall


Rest in this position for while
each day.

/. To clinch the defense OF Mos

LONDON, May 22.-Mr and Mrs.
Gilbert w. Mitchell and Grace Har-
rison, their feminine farm hand,
were decorated today for persistently
operating a Dover area farm-Brit-
aims closest to the continent-under
German shelling, machine gun fire
and bombing.


"Unexampled effort, sustained
bravery and devotion to duty" were
cited by the government. Mitchell
was awarded the George Medal,
which is presented primarily to
civilians for acts of great bravery.
His wife, Kathleen, and Miss Har-
rison were awarded the British
Empire Medal.

targets off and on for nearly two
years, are probably the most vulner-
able in all Britain. The surround.
ing acreage is stippled with filed
in shell holes.


Except for the frequent occasions
when the three have had to take
cover, the farm work has gone on
uninterruptedly.

terattacks by day, the Army of
the Nile has penetrated Field

positions and widened a road for
tank attack through enemy
minefelds, battlefront dispatches
reported today.


AS the battle for North Africa

was no word of clash between main
armored forces, but the cautious
British advance through mines,
barbed wire and fields of heavy fire
was clearing a battle ground for the
expected test.


United States Army fighters and
bombers were taking an increasing
part, along with the Raj and South
African Air Force, in holding the
mastery of the desert skies, with a
tight protective cover over the Brit
ish advance and a ruinous battering
OF enemy positions.


Advance ground forces operating
within sight of the bombing of Axis
troops and strong points sent back
their message OF praise: Good
show: keep it up"


1s Axis Planes Shot Down.

over the desert. the Mediterranean
and Malta, Allied airmen scored
18 to 10 over the Axis in planes
shot down.


United States fighters intercepted
four Macchi 202's over the desert
and knocked down all four, equalling
IN a single fight their total bag for
the day before.


United States medium bombers
dealt battering blows at Rommel's
land supply lines and his massed
tanks, and heavy bombers blew up
a merchantmen and hit a tanker
and barges in convoy attacks.

and in the air, is continuing, the
joint British Headquarters-RAF'
communique said. Eighteen Axis
planes were reported destroyed, 16

iterranean, and at least three more

strong support to the British and
Allied land forces in yesterdays
desert fighting. In one instance
two important Axis concentrations
forming for counterattack were
broken up by continuous shuttle at

bombers attacked a convoy off To-
bruk and saw one tanker burst into
flames and large merchant vessel
blow up after hits by bombs and
aerial torpedoes.

down two German escort planes
after an attack on the convoy.


The convoy attack was carried out
by planes of the United States Army

African Air Force.

included four destroyers and large
air escort. Only one Of the con-

CAIRO, Egypt, June 6-The
British Eighth Army has wrested
armored superiority from the
Germans in the Libyan desert

bridge, the crosstrah Is miles south

ish prisoners in Africa. Earlier

CHUNGKING, March 28.-The
Chinese executive Yuan announced
q national general mobilization act
today giving the government almost
unlimited power to conscript man.
power and material resources for

nese.

cific war and its effects on China's
situation and had planned and pre-
pared to meet them in anticipa-
ton Of conditions now existing"

empowered the government to COM
mandeer or seize materials ranging
from military weapons. fodder and
medical supplies to ships and all
other means of transport, electric
power, fuel, engineering apparatus
and communications equipment.


1t also empowered the government
to order for delivery all materials
vital to the prosecution of the war
or the reconstruction of the nation.
Under it the government may con-
troll prices, commander labor serv-
ices, prohibit strikes, lockouts and
picketing, determine the use of capi-
tai, regulate imports and exports
and take over and use any land or
building.

miters blasted an ice jam in the
Lackawaxen River last night and
prevented another flood in this
Northeastern Pennsylvania town of
5000, which counted Is deaths when
the river spilled over its banks last
May %.


Mountainous piles of ice. jammed
by 24-hour rain, had damned up
for mile behind temporary bridge
in the center of the town. The river
was tapping at the top of its retain
ing walls, feet above normal level,
when hastily mobilized State high
way crews began blasting a channel
to carry of the pent-up water.


The dynamiting continued several
hours and early today police said the
flood threat had been eliminated.


In low-land sections, anxious
householders had moved belongings
from the first floors of their homes.
Crowds gathered in the streets and
the atmosphere was tense until word
spread that the jam had been
broken.

After Caesar returned to Rome,
Cleopatra made a journey there.
She hoped to marry Caesar, and
thus to share the power over the
whole Roman empire, instead of
ruling only a single country.


The Egyptian queen failed in her
object. Two years after going back
to Rome, Julius Caesar was mur-
dered.


That event brought on new war
fare, and years passed before it be-
came clear who would take his
place. Even then the power was
divided between three men-a good
friend of Caesar named Mark
Antony, general named Lepidus,
and young man known as Oc-
tavian.


Meanwhile Cleopatra once more
had taken up residence in Egypt.
She was at this time the only mon
arch OF the country, no longer hav-
ing brother with whom she needed
to share the power.


Mark Antony had arranged to
rule the eastern end of the Roman
empire, and it seemed plain that he
meant to take the Egyptian throne
away from Cleopatra. That lady,
however, had other ideas.


Meeting Mark Antony, she
charmed him-perhaps even more
strongly than she had charmed
Julius Caesar. For II years she
helped him rule his share of the
empire.


A sharp end came to the story of
Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian,
who had made his home in Rome,
opened war against his partner
After winning an important sea
battle, Octavian entered Egypt,
Antony and Cleopatra took their
own lives. We are told that Cleo
patra died after letting an asp crawl
from a basket and bite her. In
later years. Octavian ruled the
Roman empire under the name of
Augustus.

BY the ASsoclAted Press.


LONDON, Nov. 9.-The North
African landings were the first
big scale combat test for some
of the United States Army's new
equipment, such as landing
barges and Garand rifles, as web
as for it's new methods of organi-
zation and operation.
] Unlike the landing in France in
the last war, American troop trans
ports could not be brought up to
friendly, commodious port for the
soldiers to march ashore in orderly
file.


This time 1t. Gen. Dwight Eisen-
hower's men were prepared for
every kind of opposition.


There was an aerial umbrella of
planes to soften up points of de-
fense. Parachute troops dropped
down to seize vital points until
other air-borne and ground troops
arrived.


With the way thus paved, the
transports, guarded by naval and
air forces, moved up offshore where
their cargoes Of men and machines
were unloaded into armored, shall
low-draft landing barges which
churned up to the beaches and
dropped their vertical prows to
serve as gangplanks. Then the
men splashed ashore.


The basic weapon of the indi-
vioual soldier is the new Garard
rife. Semi-automatic, cooked from
the discharged energy of the pre-
vious shot, the Garand fires several
times faster than the bolt-action
Springfield.


With tanks and ank-destroyer
vehicles rumbling off the barges and
blazing the way, the infantry piles
into armored trucks and dashes for
objectives miles inland, or moves
afoot-not in picture book forma-
ton. but in widely dispersed order,
ducking and crawling behind trees,
shrubs, rocks and even clumps Of
grass and weed against immediate
points of resistance.


That is how the United States
Army today makes a landing-air-
men, naval forces, parachute troops,
air-bor troops, Rangers, engineers,
infantry, armored divisions, tank de-
stroyer battalions and specialists of
all kinds neatly co-ordinated.

The war in the South Pacific is as
complex as it is far-fung. Extend
ing over millions of square miles of
island-studded ocean, it has many
phases and at least three strategical
aSpects-those of land, sea and air.
For the moment, land fighting holds
the spotlight and centers around the
tactically separate yet Strategically
connected operations on Guadal-
canal Island in the SolomonS and in
the New Guinea hills back of Port
Moresby. In both those areas, savage
battles are being fought between
relatively small, yet highly special
lied units. And the outcome appar-
emily will be determined by the
relative skill and stamina of the
respective forces.


Probably the greatest single sur
prise of the Pacific war has been the
extraordinary ability of Japans
jungle troops. First in Malaga and
then in Burma, they applied infiltra-
ton tactics which quickly over
whelmed their British and East
Indian opponents. Much the same
was true in the Netherlands Indies
And it begins to look as though his
tory might repeat itself in New
Guinea. During the past ten days
the Japanese jungle specialists have
made an amazing series of advances,
first across the reputedly impreg-
nable Owen Stanley Mountains, and
then through the rugged foothills
between the main range and the sea-
coast. In the past three days they
have gone fully twenty miles
through terrain covered with sup
posedly impenetrable jungle, and
they have accomplished all this
against the stubborn opposition of
veteran Australian troops who are
also jungle-wise. They are now half
way from the mountains to Port
Moresby, the main Allied base in New
Guinea which covers the approach





At Guadalcanal the situation is
thus far less disquieting. Guadal-
canal is large island, nearly one
hundred miles long and averaging
between thirty and forty miles broad.
The interior is hilly to mountainous
and, for the most part, clad in heavy
ivy, Eor1yy i,a AI1o,,cf bow ,,oiofc
on the coast, together with a half
completed airfield, were captured by
our Marines as part of the brilliant
surprise operation which took the
Southern Solomons The remnant of
the Japanese garrison of Guadal-
canal was driven into the interior,
where they were systematically
hunted by our forces. However, they
were never eXterminated, and re-
Gently they have been heavily REIN
forced by japanese troops landed
probably by speedboats under cover
of darkness. Although the airfield
and coastal points are still in our
possession, it looks as though the
jungle hinterland was mostly in Jap
anese control. Whether our forces
on Guadalcanal were not strong
enough to maintain the offensive
against the strengthened Japanese,
or whether the latter's infiltration
tactics through, the dense jungle
succeeded there as on New Guinea,
has not yet been revealed by our
communiques.


One thing, however, appears GER
tain. The highly trained Japanese
jungle fighters are opponents so
dangerously resourceful that none
but the best troops can cope with
them on that difficult terrain. It is
now known that the Japanese high
command has been training large
units for years in this highly spe-
cialized type of warfare, their train
ing grounds being Formosa and
Southern China, where semi i-tropical
jungle country is abundantly found.
That is one more proof of the metic-
ulous care with which the war lords
of Toxic prepared for the gigantic
gamble they have undertaken.

WHITEHORSE, Yukon Territory
Jan. 28.-Two occupants of a plane
missing for days between here and
an Alaskan airport have reached
Fort Yukon, Alaska, safely after a
walk down the ice of the Porcupine
River, where they landed when their
plane ran out of fuel.


The airmen reported they had lost
their bearings while en- route to
Alaska but flew on for nine hours.
When their gasoline tanks ran dry,
they made safe landing on the
river ice. Still lost, they followed
the winding river and arrived at
Fort Yukon Monday night.


Names of the men were not given.

BY the Associated Press.


MEXICO CITY, Sept. 8.-The
6,511-ton Mexican tanker Amatlan,
torpedoed and sunk in the Gulf OF
Mexico, was disclosed today to have
been navigating at her own risk
after sailing from Havana without
asking for naval protection.


The loss of the tanker and the
fact that 10 crew members were
missing were announced yesterday
by her owners, the Mexican Petro-
leum Co.


Gen. Juan F. Azcarate, chief of
staff of the Gulf of Mexico defense
zone, disclosed she had not asked
for naval protection and said no
Mexican ships had been torpedoed
while under Mexican naval and air
force escort since the convoy system
was established.


The Amatlan was the sixth ship
flying the Mexican flag to be sunk
by Axis submarines.

Sailed at Her Own Risk

returned with a clothes pin, the
only property left.


Large scale and systematic loot
ing of Hong Kong Island got un-
der way as soon as the colony sur
rendered. Rich residences in the

mer servants.

sioner.

The cause of volcanic eruptions
is one of the earth's mysteries which
scientists have never satisfactorily
solved. Although there are many
theories about volcanoes, We know
little of the actual causes.


Rocks beneath the surface Of the
earth are kept moist by the water
that seeps through. The heat is
very intense beneath these layers
Of rocks, because the earth's temper
ature increases as its center is ap-
preached. Gradually, steam is pro-
duced, and its pressure increases
constantly.


At the same time, gases are formed
by the decomposition of rocks and
water, and as the molten material
from below spreads over the watery
rocks near the surface, it combines
with the gases. AS the mass reaches
the surface, the weight of the rocks
above cannot hold in the expanding
steam, and the whole mass explodes
The molten NEUTRALITY-SUSPICIOUS. out
and the gases escape. Both the flow
ing lava and the gases mean sure
death for any living thing caught in
their path.

always contained stepping stones

By 1871 enormous increases in the
efficiency of weapons, especially aerial
weapons, had greatly decreased Amer.
ica'S invulnerabllitV. Whoever controlled

ington calling for American protection of

nounced American armed forces had also

Guiana, the South American possession

CAIRO, Sept. 2.-British forces
were locked heavily in battle
with Axis armor all day yester-

quarters announced today.


The war bulletin. issued jointly
by the headquarters and the Raj
said United States Army Air Force
planes participated in extensive air

which an Allied battle line was
braced against the expected shock
of Field Marshal Erwin Rommel's S
powerful tank forces, again trying to
grind forward toward Alexandria, the
Nile and the Suez Canal.


The readiness of the Allies to meet
Marshal Rommel's challenge was
Indicated by the communicates re-
port that British forces made their
own sally Monday night on the
northern flank of the Ell Alamein
line and brought back batch of
German prisoners.


Swirling Sand Beclouds Battle.


Ground action yesterday centered
between the Ruweisat Ridge in the
center and Ell Himeimat, on the
southern wing near the Qattara De-
preston, the bulletin added.


Despite swirling sand beclouding
the battle zone, it said, the Allies
air coverage was on a large scale
and the hail of bombs which fell on
the enemy was both intensive and
accurate"


"At least two large Stuka forma-
tions were attacked by our fighters
and the enemy was on many occa-
sions forced to jettison his bombs, I"
the bulletin said


During the day at least six enemy
bombers and five fighters were de-
stroyed in these operations.


More than dozen were dam
aged. Our long-range fighters sue
cessfully attacked enemy motor
transport on the coastal road be-
tween Gambut and Sidi Barrani"


Marshal Rommel had concen-
trated the German armor in the
south and penetrated the low desert
land between the Ell Ruweisat ridge
In the north center and the 600-foot
height of Ell Himeimat to the south
near the Quattara Depression.


The direction of battle still was
Unclear but it appeared that the
German tactician hoped to out
flank the British along the Ell
Ruweisat ridge which roughly paral-
lels the Mediterranean at right
angle to the El Alamein line.


The main battle is now engaged in
this valley" which is studded with
British mines.


The opposing forces tend to face
each other north and south rather
than east and west, though Marshal
Rommel's spearhead had made some
progress directly to the east.


This eastward thrust has not yet
reached alarming proportions.


Dust Storms Over Desert.


Dust storms, made danser by the
tanks and vehicles churning on the
loose desert sands, blew SpaSmodl-
cally over the battlefield and ham,
pered Allied air support. which
nevertheless was strong from dawn
to dusk.


The United States Air Force once
more played an important part
aiongside British and South African
squadrons.


BY midday yesterday seven sep
arate bomber formations with large
fighter escorts had scored important
successes against the attacking
enemy.


At various times nearly all the
Allied formations were attacked by
Axis interceptors, but American
fighters effectively protected the
bombers. The enemy was using very
large formations of Stuka dive
bombers escorted by Messerschmitt-
zoos.


Rommel Uses 500 800 Tanks.


Backing up his assault on the Brit
ish lines near Ell Himeimat with an
estimated 500 to 600 tanks, Marshal
Rommel probed the Allied positions
initially for soft spot which might
open a road to the Nile.


One of his spearheads was report
ed to have advanced miles through
the dangerous Allied mine fields ano
one of the worst duststorms of the
war.

turned north after striking eastward

column branched off to the south
reports from the front said.

commander of the 9th Army, ap'
parently was holding back his mair

said, probably outnumbered that o

SOMEWHERE IN AUSTRALIA,
July 1.-Japanese bases in New
Britain and New Guinea were at
tackled by strong forces of Allied
bombers before dawn yesterday
in the largest raid in several
days, it was disclosed tonight by
airmen who participated in the
attack.

planes bombed Rabaul, on New
Britain, where large fires were start
ed among installations in the wharf
area, they said.


One bomber was reported to have
made several runs over its target
despite heavy anti-aircraft fire,
leaving blaze which was visible for
20 miles through the overhanging
haze.

said, other bombers attacked Luka-
mai Airport, near Rabaul, dropping
demolition bombs on runways and
buildings.


Heavy clouds prevented observa-
ton of the results. The runways at
Lac, New Guinea, were also attacked
but ground haze and a dim moon
made the effects undesirable, the
bomber pilots reported.

Seven new aircraft carriers of a

chusetts yard are the Cabot, Bunker
Hill, Oriskany and Ticonderoga.

launched and the Mobile, Biloxi
and Vicksburg.


When these II aircraft carriers

will have a total of 18 carriers for
active duty. Seven are already on
duty with the fleets: The Lexing
ton and Saratoga, both converted
from warships, the Ranger, Enter
prise, Hornet, Wasp and Yorktown.

Australians have retired to the
cannibal- Infested hills to become
raiding bush rangers-a modern
versions of the Kelly gang and other
famous bandit organizations which
roamed the Australian bush half
century ago.


They swoop on the Japanese at
night and their frequent raids have
forced the Japs to hug the coast
where they have established bases.

MOSCOW, Aug. 22.-Their faces
black from the rays of the burning
sun and the dust of battle, hundreds
of old Cossack warriors, with their
women and children were driving
an endless stream of livestock into
the Caucasus mountains today
rather than let them fall to the
Germans.


The Cossacks have been in many
wars" growled 80-year-old Nikolai
Dmitrivish Onuprienko to a Red
Star correspondent. They never
have become prisoners"


His daughter tugged at the old
mans jacket that bore four ancient
crosses of ST. George and one of the
Red banner.


Come along, father, we must
hurry" she told him. The grum-
bling old warrior trudged along
while the women and boys rode
oxen and cows, driving their sheep,
hogs and chickens ahead.


The Red Star account was the
first story of the mass exodus of the
Cossacks from their beloved Kuban
villages.


Refugees Rush to Mountains.


The roads are hot. The sun beats
down. The trees are still green and
the lush fields of wheat, corn, sun
flowers and tobacco still wave
gently in fitful breezes as the sad
dened columns of refugees hurry
toward the sanctuary of the noun
tains


A bedlam of noise was reported
over great areas as the long columns
moved down the roads. Women.
children and old men constantly
were hurrying along believing cows.
hogs and bleating sheep.


The CoSSacks were moving everv-
thing movable int othe mountains
determined the Germans would get
nothing, the army newspaper said.
They even hastily raided laden
trees in the orchard.


Red Army trucks carrying bombs.
shells and wounded flashed up and
down the roads, threading the lines
of refugees. The report said the
refugees were clogging some high
ways. This is easily understand
able to any one who has Travelled
a Russian road.


Military trucks slow down for
nothing. Some of the world s
widest drivers operate them. When
a civilian sees truck coming he
gets off the road "sechas
ing Immediately.


Village Sent 400 Men.
The refugee columns passed
through Cossack villages whence
hundreds have gone to fight since
July. At one village, the people
told the Red Star reporter thai
horsemen galloped off in saddle.
belonging to their grandfathers anc
| swinging sabers that had passed
down to them through the genera
tions.


Petro Putrusenko was one O.
these. He told how his village hae
sent 400 men, some of them 5,
years old, to the front.


Sadly the columns moved on to
ward the high Caucasus mountains


Some women complained tina
they wanted to stay at the front
pointing out that the Cossacks don
belong in the rear when wars ar
about. But wiser counsel persuade,
them that this is the way to VIII
the new type war-what you can
not burn you take with you, leavin
the invader as little as you can.
| Above the noise of the cattl
along the dusty roads bearing tn
footprints OF war came cry lik
a chorus. eve will be back"
| Onward they went, disappearin
into long shadows of the snow
capped Caucasus ranges.

DAVIS, Calf, Oct. 30.-You may
have to eat your spinach and carrots
and like them If the manpower
shortage and the need for dietary
essentials become extreme, three
University Of California agricultural
experts asserted yesterday.


They surveyed the major vegetable
crops to find which ones yielded the
most vitamins, minerals and calories
per acre and per man-hour of labor,
with the idea of determining what
could be planted to get the most
eficient production in case of q
real food crisis.


Spinach took first place on both
lists-acreage yield and work per
acre. Carrots stood high on the list.


When labor was taken into ac-
count, the vitamin- -mineral-calorie
yield stood in this order: Spinach,
winter squash, Irish potatoes, cab
bage, carrots, canning tomatoes,
caulifiower and lettuce.


In yield per acre, not considering
the amount Of work required, the
most eficient producers of these
necessary nutritional elements were,
respectively, spinach, onions, Irish
potatoes, celery, winter squash, cab
bage, broccoli and cauliflower.


The experts, John H. MacGillivray,
G. c. Hanna and p A. Minges, said
their findings indicated certain
vegetable crops-they did not specify
which ones-possibly should be elm
mated from production If the farm
labor and equipment situation be-
came critical.


They said palatability and con-
sumer preferences were less i'm
portant than agricultural economy
and dietary value in the war emer-
gency.

ginia, a project in which the Coast

text:
Momentous changes in the mill
tary situation during the past week
indicate that the supreme test Of the
winter campaign in Russia may be
at hand. It Is now nearly two
months since the Red Armies began
their general counteroffensive, nice
ly timed when the last German Often
sive had fought itself to standstill
amid the early rigors of the Russian
winter, which caught the Germans
exhausted, i'll clad, with dangerously
extended salients and with congested
supply lines.


Paced by crack Siberian corps,
fresh and Splendidly equipped, the
Russian offensive gained initial sue
cesses which imperiled the German
pincer arms and caused them heavy
losses. However, the German high
command Strengthened their lines
with the obvious intention of retreat
ing slowly to defensible front which
they could hold until spring. For a
solid month the Russians hammered
the slowly retiring Germans, doing
them much damage, yet nowhere
breaking down the stubborn defense.


Then, Just week ago, the scene
changed sharply in the Russians
favor. The pivotal German strong
hold of Mozhaisk, within striking
distance Of Moscow, fell before q
tremendous frontal attack combined
with pincer movements against what
had become an exposed salient.
The survivors of the 100000 de-
tenders are now retreating along the
main railroad and highway to Wanna
and Smolensk.


This, in itself, Is not q disaster.
What imperils the entire German
central front is the first real Rus
sian break-through to the north
ward, which, despite deep snow and
40 below zero cold, has already
driven 10 miles. Here the Russian
advance guards stand far to the west
Of Smolensk and due south of Lenin-
grad, at point where they claim to
have cut the main north-south rail-
way line from Leningrad to the
Ukraine, which Is the chief German
lateral communication line. Further
more, the Russians here are only so
miles from the other trunk railway
which supplies their northern armies
besieging Leningrad This Russian
break-through not only imperils the
German northern and central army
groups, but has been made in con-
junction with q second Russian ad-
vance south of Mozhaisk which
threatens to grip the German
ma-Smolensk line in a gigantic
pincers movement. Unless the Ger
mans can check both these sweeping
Russian advances, their entire east
ern front, as now constituted, will
be In jeopardy and a general retreat
under terrible climatic handicaps can
alone save them from repeated en-
circlements and destruction in detail.


The Russian winter is now ap-
preaching its peak of cold, while the
heaviest snowfall comes in February
and early March. The Germans
must face at least two months when
their handicaps on both men and
equipment will be most severe. This
is the grim ordeal they must weather
against an enemy flushed with sue
cess and determined to make the
most of every advantage.

The War Department today
ordered eliminated the pre-in-
duction period in which selectees
could wind up their affairs after
they were sure they were phys
ically qualified for Army service.


In the future, the War Depart
ment announced, selectees will be
inducted into the Army at the time
of their physical examination.


1t has been known for some time
that the Navy and Marine Corps
have been enlisting number of
men qualified for Army induction
after they had received their physi-
cal examinations. 1t was under
stood that the new system, which
reverts to the procedure originally
followed with slight difference,
was ordered to prevent men from
volunteering for Navy or Marine
Corps service after they were sure
they would be inducted into the
Army within few days.


Difference In Procedure.


The only difference between this
and the original procedure is that
originally men passed strict local
board physical examination in the
course of processing" while under
the new system local boards will
continue to give screening" ex-
aminations rejecting the obviously
physically unfit only.


The rough screening replaced the
strict local board physical examina-
tions. when the selective service sys-
tenn started giving men a Today no.
tice period after their Army physical
examinations.


Originally, selectees were classified
in la after they passed their local
board physicals; were given a Today
appeal period and then local boards
notified them that they would be in
Quoted in 10 days. On the day of
induction they took their Army
physical examinations.


This was replaced by the pro-
cedure now in operation when the
Army started rejecting large num-
berc Of men sent for induction after
they had resigned their jobs and
MADE all arrangements for leaving
civilian life. To eliminate this dis
ruption. the second system was
adopted. Men were given the rough
screening. allowed 10 days for ap-
peal, ordered to take their Army
physical and were given another 10
| days, after the local boards had re-
ceived the physical examination re-
ports, before they were ordered to re-
port for induction.


Immediate Furloughs.
Henceforth, registrants will be
given a notice of induction instead
of notice to report for their Army
physicals. After the Army physicals,
those who pass will be indicted i'm
mediately. Those rejected will be
sent back to civilian life to get back
their jobs and begin unwinding their
affairs.


The War Department has assured
the selective service system that in
cases where immediate induction
would cause undue hardships, the
registrant will be given an imme-
diate furlough to adjust his civilian
affairs. 1t was understood, however.
that the man would have to resign
his job and make all possible other
adjustments before he reported for
his physical examination.


The new procedure will not inter-
fere with the registrant's right to
appeal. The only difference will be
that he will have no time to make
adjustments after he knows he is
going to be called.

Thousands Face Draft.


The governments latest drastic
DEGREES make thousands of Aus.
tralians liable to a labor draft or
army terms and at army pay.


The new wartime edicts were
aimed at profiting from the lessons
Australia has learned from the wal
in the Pacific so far-the urgent
need for fast, uninterrupted and
plentiful production and for pre-
cision military cooperation.


These were summarized in yester-
days report of Maj. Gen. Henry
Gordon Bennett. the Australian
commander at Singapore who es-
capped the Japanese. He told the
Commonwealth Council, which ap-
parently responded quickly to his
advice, that the campaign in Malaga
proved the need of modern army
for crushing aerial superiority
working in close collaboration with
the land forces.


Five Holidays Abolished.


Besides calling civilians for COM
pulsory service, the government also
abolished five major holidays and
welded the Australian imperial force
the famous volunteer army, into one
unit with the militia and the per-
manent garrison.


The decision to extend the labor
corps system meant compulsory
service at army pay-well below
trade union levels-and under vlr-
tual army discipline, chiefly for
work on construction and mainte-
nance projects.


These measures projected Austria
Ian readiness yet another long step
forward


Two Holidays Remain.


Non-essentials already have been
trimmed from civilian life, some ra-
tioning has been instituted, the
blackout has been organized and
military rule and civilian evacua-
ton enforced in Northern Austria
liza. --- s~--


The groundwork for marshalling
all resources had been prepared last
month in regulations providing for
full mobilization of services and
property.


The only holidays which will be
permitted until July will be Good
Friday and Easter. Those eliminat-
ed are Labor Day. which Australia
normally observes this month: East
er Monday and Easter Tuesday, An
zac Day on April Is, and the Kings S
birthday in June.

WITH UNITED STATES FORCES
IN TUNISIA, Dec. 13 Delayed
Sticky brown mud has added a new
factor to the Allied North African
campaign which now, at least
temporarily, has settled down to
one of fixed positions while both
Allies and Axis rush up men and
materiel for the gigantic battle
which will be fought on the ap-
proaches to Tunis.


The beginning of the winter rainy
season, with the resultant muck,
undoubtedly has added to the diff
culties OF both sides, but the British
and American forces probably are
feeling the drag of mud on wheels
and tracks more because of the
longer lines of land communications.


Track and half-track vehicles
which formerly set out across the
country with as much ease as on
highways now are begging down.


Become Real Problem.


Steep and narrow roads, difficult
for motor transport at best, have
become a real problem as the rains
have softened their shoulders and
slickened their clay surfaces.


Tanks and heavy vehicles return
ing to bivouacs in fields and on hill
sides have left layers of mud on
paved roads, giving them rough,
slippery and dangerous surfaces.


Officers say, however, that the
number Of night accidents has been
small, particularly in view of the
conditions. Wrecker and reclama-
ton services have been excellent and
maintenance depots usually have
disabled trucks back in running
order in few hours.


In one dawn drive saw numerous
overturned trucks-but on the drive
back over the same road at noon
not one remained.


Arab labor under the direction of
our French allies has been put to
work strengthening road shoulders
and erecting guards on dangerous
curves


Shovels Used by Troops.


Troops with shovels have been
used on difficult sectors where mud
was interfering with urgent trans
port.


Ofhcers and men who are adjust
ing themselves to living in the mire
and wearing a permanent crust of
dried mud on their clothing and
shoes say that the United States
equipment sis holding up very we'll
under the new hardships."
Jeeps and trucks with four wheel
drives turned to improvised tracks
across fields without dimculty, where
ordinary vehicles begged down
Immediately.

BY the Associated Press.


CHUNGKING, China, April l.
Three 100-man Chinese survey
corps, each including engineers, doc
tors, road experts, mapmakers and
armed guards, will leave Running
shortly to map a temporary coolie
and animal transport route to India
over which gasoline and other vital
materials can be rushed to China
while the new India road is being
completed.


This emergency scheme, necessi-
tated by the japanese drive into
Burma which closed the Burma
road, calls for the use of pack
trains, human caravans, mule and
man-drawn carts and even ele-
plants over route following a gen.
eral line from Western Yunnan
Province through upper Burma to
India.


The surveyors admittedly are
tackling a tough Job, for they must
work through one of the widest
regions in the world. Various dis
eases. notably malignant malaria,
prevail the year round, while the
terrain to be crossed also abounds
In hostile tribes, wild animals and
poisonous insects.


Another route being considered
would lead northwest from Kun
ming into Sikang Province and then
through Tibet.


Besides its surveying equipment
and road-building material, each
corps must carry enough food for
one or two months, as through many
mountain and jungle stretches there
are no human habitations. On the
homeward trip the corps will bring
back war supplies.


This will be China's first foreign
extension of its primitive pack
train transport system in modern
times. China possesses 40 main and
branch lines of this kind covering
1900 miles in Is provinces. Plans

NEW DELHI, India. March 27.
-Mohandas K. Gandhi, Indian
leader, met this afternoon with
Sir Stafford Cripps, Britain's
special emisSary.


The little nationalist leader came
here from his humble retreat in
Wardha to confer with Sir Stafford,
entrusted by the British war cabi-
net with seeking unanimous Indian
acceptance of Britain's proposals
for greater autonomy for India
and Indian support for Britain's war
effort.


Gandhi's talk with Sir Stafford
lasted two hours and 10 minutes. 1t
was the longest the Briton has had
so far with any of the several un-
official Indian leaders he has met.


The Indian leader was attired In
his customary loin cloth, with a
shawl draped around his shoulders
He arrived alone by automobile. and
was greeted warmly by Sir Stafford


At the same time the working
committee of the Moslem League
met to consider the British pro-
posals as communicated to its
leader, Mohamed Ali Jinnah.


Congress party circles expressed
belief a frank exchange of ideas
between Cripps and Gandhi might
speed deliberations of the party's
Working Committee, which will con.
slider the proposals Sunday.


While details of the British plan
remained secret, there was a general
feeling in political quarters that the
leaders Of both the Congress Party
and the Moslem League had found
the fundamental principles salts
factory.


The working parties of the two
committees, 1t was believed, probably
will be concerned chiefly with sug-
gesting adjustments which might
prove helpful in the practical ex.
ecution of these principles.

text:
Once, long, long ago, Jupiter loved
a beautiful earthly maiden named
Mistle. Because Jupiter was god
he could not marry her. Mistle,
however, did not pine away because
of this, but married a courageous
youth. At the wedding feast she
carried lovely bouquet of flowers
which she laid down as she was
about to greet her guests.


Mistle grew pale when Jupiter,
attending the feast unseen by any
of the guests, stole the bouquet and
glided back to his home in the sky.
He intended to keep the flowers as
a memento of their love. Jove knew
of this love, and seeing the flowers,
snatched them from his hands and
angrily flung them down to the
earth. The poor little bouquet
hurtled through the air and would
have been dashed to pieces had not
the great oak, in sympathy, reached
out its branches and caught the
trembling flowers.


And ever since that time the
mistletoe has .clung to the oak tree
and forever bears its small, gray
green leaves and pale, waxy berries
in memory of the. lovely maiden
whom Jupiter once loved.

LONDON, Oct. 2.-The German
controlled Paris press opened a cam
paign yesterday to bring France into
q military alliance with the Axis
and clear. the way for German aid
In the defense" Of the French
African Empire.


The Paris radio has made repeated

ences have been held among Vichy
military chiefs and colonial admin
istrators on defense problems.

were blockading Dakar, dispatches
from Vichy told of French ship
movements off the port, presumably
In prepara ton for evacuation.


simultaneously Vichy announced

women and children from Dakar.

Lisbon reported that the Vichy gov
ernment had consented ito German
control over all French airlines and
had granted Germany unrestricted
right to use equipment and airdrome

Representative of the German

Had she been allowed to follow

anese forces or before the Japanese

May 1.-Two unidentified war
planes, obviously japanese, have
flown over the vulnerable north
east coast of Australia indicating
that Japan may soon strike at the
continent and give American
forces here their first test of bat
tie. Gen. Douglas Macarthur re-
vealed today.


Macarthur announced in a spe-
cial communique that the planes
had flown over Townsville, on the
populated coastal fringe, and that
attempts TO intercept them had
failed.


II was the first time that en-
envy planes had been definitely re-
ported over the populated area,
though there had been uncon-
firmed reports of such reconnais-
sance fights before Macarthur as
sumed his command of American,
Australian and Netherlands forces
In Australia.


The fact that Townsville is more
than 1000 miles from the nearest
Japanese land bases, raised the
question whether the planes were
carrier-borne. and meant that an
enemy feet was within striking
distance OF the continent.


Flying at high altitude. the
planes passed safely over a bar
rage put up by Allied anti-aircraft
guns and disappeared before
American and Australian inter-
ceptor planes could contact them.


The Importance which MacAr-
thur attached TO the visit of the
planes, almost certainly japanese
reconnaissance craft. was empha-
sized by the fact that he made il
his first special communique.


Townsville is on the vitality inn
portant east coast railroad-high-
way communication line. 700 miles
north of Brisbane and 1000 miles
west OF Free French New Cafe
donia where American forces are
now based.


Sighting of the planes came al
a moment when the fierce aerial
warfare in the northeastern inva-
sion zone was reaching a peak.

his inspection of the building he
discovered:

type were upset and walls smeared
with ink; in the woodworking room,
motors were torn loose from several
power tools, work benches over
turned, tools scattered about and
walls daubed with wood stains; in
the cooking room, kitchen utensils
were thrown about and food scat
tered over the floor.


Mr. Adamick estimated the dam
age at $4,000 and said 10 workmen
were assigned to clean the wreckage.


Sergt. Miller said two of the boys
were students at Peabody, while the
third attended another school.

LONDON, Dec. 23-For the last
week, reports have been emanating
from Ankara suggesting that new.
impressive steps are impending be-
tween Turkey and Russia. placing
their relations on a firmer basis of
friendship 1t also has been as
serted that this new step, whatever
1t might be, would be Endorsed for
mally by the United States. Some
American news agencies filing from
Ankara have even declared that the
United States was offering some
form Of guarantee.


These reports coincided with the
arrival back in Ankara of American
Ambassador Laurence A. Stein
hardt. But for this fact, London
would not have been particularly in
terested. Careful inquiries show
that these reports were largely fab
ricated following sudden spate OF
rumors circulating in Ankara but
not having any solid foundation.


Your correspondent understands
that Mr. Steinhardt personally has
done everything possible to discour-
age these stories. but has not sue
ceeded in dissuading enterprising
reporters from sending out variety
of sensational versions.


Chess Session Discounted.


One largely advertised piece of
confirmatory evidence quoted is the
fact that Soviet Ambassador Vino
gradov, lately returned from a visit
! TO Moscow, spent three hours play
ing chess with Turkish Foreign
Minister Saracoglu and concluded
, that the men were talking profound
affairs of state. Actually, there was
nothing unusual in this game to
which both men are addicted and at
which they frequently enjoy hong
sessions.


Though 1t is less intriguing than
the versions sent out, your CORE
spondent has the best of reasons for
asserting that business was not
talked that day. While it is desir-
able to discount the impression tina
something sensational is pending. it
is .nonetheless. true that Russo
Turkish relations actually have been
undergoing steady. progressive i'm
provement recently. and certainly
Britain and the United States alike
warmly welcome this fact and are
constantly doing their utmost to en-
courage it.


Turkeys geographical position and
long standing belief that Russia
coveted a sphere of influence in the
Balkans has made the Turks sus-
picious of their great and powerful
northern neighbor But the actual
course OF the war and the recent
growth of confidence and under
standing between London and Mos
COW have had reassuring influence
in Ankara.


Would Resist Axis Attack.


The Russians. for their part, now
seem convinced that Turkey. while
determined to maintain outwardly
the most correct neutrality. will GER
tainly defend herself against any
Axis attack This has been strongly
underlined by indignant articles ap-
pearing in the Turkish press reject
ing the recent warning of Hitlers
Voelkischer Beobachter that coun-
tries attempting to act against Ger
many would end up like Poland.
The Turks consider this definitely
aimed against their country and
warn: No Europe country. espe-
cially Turkey, will submit to enslave-
ment by Germany"


One leading Turkish newspape
YeniSabah. commented Instead of
occupying themselves with dreams.
the Germans would better pray for
victory. At present the Allies are
beating hell out of them in Africa"


Allied supplies, including notably

ing the Turkish forces in important
amounts and the Turks feel more
confident of their ability to back up
words by actions, but there is not the
slightest reason to think they will
voluntarily abandon neutrality.

Concern over our endangered ma
rines and soldiers on Guadalcanal
island should not obscure in our
larger vision the new peril which
menaces the heroic city on the Volga.
We do not know whether German
intimations that direct assaults on
Stalingrad would be discontinued
were misleading propaganda or
whether the German high command
has changed it's mind. Certain it is,
however, that infantry and tank
attacks have been renewed with full
scale fury, though on restricted
front.


The point selected is the industrial
area at Stalingrad's northern ex-
tremity. Here is located the great
Dzherzhinski tractor plant, together
with other important factories and a.
workers settlement of apartment
houses, all solidly built of reinforced
concrete and brick construction.
Though badly battered by Axis bonn
bardments, these structures are like
nest of fortresses which have hith-
erto defied all assaults. Now, how
ever, the German Army communique
claims that the tractor plant has
been taken and the Volga reached on
a two-mile front, though it admits
that some isolated factories still hold
out and that the Red Army CON
tinues to fight as if nothing had hap
pened." These German claims are
partially confirmed by Moscow dis
patches which admit a withdrawal
from one of the city's settlements"
which can mean only the industrial
area above described.


. The Axis strategy involved in this
new advance is clear. Possession of
Northern Stalingrad would mean an
Axis bulwark against Timoshenkos
forces driving across the open coun-
try still farther to the northward,
which were recently reported to have
reached a point from which the city
itself could be seen. For the last two
days, however, this relieving opera
ton has made no perceptible prog
ress. That is an equally disquieting
aspect of tense situation. Red
Star, the Soviet Army organ, admits
the gravity of the crisis when it
writes: THE vile enemy aims to
capture the city at any cost. The
decisive battle for Stalingrad is
going on"


The stakes involved in the siege of
this key city on the Volga have been
so frequently and fully analyzed dur
ing the hectic eight weeks which
have now elapsed since the Axis
armies launched their first attacks
that they are obvious to all observers.
The Germans still have a full month
before real winter weather sets in.
because the freeze line" does not
ordinarily reach Stalingrad until
about November 20. The weather is
already chilly, but the Germans pre-
sumably are equipped for cold
weather, since they must winter there
or in the vicinity, no matter how the
siege turns out. The coming weeks
probably will witness what Red Star
aptly terms the decisive" phase of
the long struggle.

ANKARA, June 15.-Twenty-one
United States airmen whose bombers
made forced landings in Turkey
after reported raids on German-held
Black Sea bases (and possibly Ru-
manian oil flelds) gave al account
of their sensational flight yesterday
to United States Ambassador Lau-
renee A. Steinhardt.


The Ambassador interviewed the
eirmen, who have been interned by
the Turkish government, and sup
piled them with money, drinks and
cigarettes.


Both American and British au-
thorities here refused any state
ment concerning the flight by the
Americans.


The airmen expressed apprecia-
ton at the treatment they were re-
ceiving from the Turkish govern
ment. 1t was understood they prob
ably would be allowed out of intern
ment on parole soon.


The Americans were in four
bombers, each carrying a crew of
seven. Some were reported
wounded.


The planes were forced down last
Friday, week after the United
States declared war on Rumania.
I, Officially, all information was
lacking here on why the craft were
flying over Turkish territory, where
they came from or where they were
going.


Reports from Turkey to London
said the planes were believed to have
been used in attacks on Odessa and
Nikolaev, German-occupied Russian
Black Sea ports. Still another re-
port said they also bombed the
nearby Rumanian oil fields.


In its first wild furry of contra
dieting reports on the forced land
ings, the German radio said the
bombers had been chased across the
Turkish border from the Sevastopol
front, indicating they might have
taken part in the continuing battle
for that Soviet Black Sea naval base.

animal-drawn vehicles wherever

trips; insist on utilizing maximum
pay load; maintain power plants

Meanwhile, the men in the air.

ground unwrapped the rifles and
ammunition. GunnerS were posted

fense force was organized the white
men waved good-by to the flyers.

Quito.


The flyers learned later by radio
that the Indians attacked as soon
as the plane disappeared. The
naked savages, however, encoun-
tered gunflre from well-placed posts
about the camp and were driven
into a wild retreat.


The next day the camp resumed
its usual work routine, the Shell Oil
Co. reported. So far the savages
have not ventured another attack.

MOSCOW, Nov. 21.-Some of the

MEXICO CITY, April 9.-Mexico
has launched a sweeping campaign
to eradicate any fifth-column men
ace from the Gulf shore.


Soon after the Interior Ministry
ordered all Axis nationals to prepare
Immediately to move inland, federal
police last night raided the homes
and Offices of German residents in
Tampico.


At least six Germans were taken
into custody, and they, along with
about 300 seized letters bearing Ger
man postmarks. are to be sent here.


The lead for the Tampico raid
came from Germans previously ar
rested, who had admitted carrying
out fifth column orders" from Ber-
lin. One object of the search was
an undercover radio transmitter.


Besides being an important port
in itself and transit point between
the United States. Central America
and the Panama Canal, Tampico is
in an area where Mexico's rich oil
fields and most important refineries
are concentrated.


The expulsion order will affect
hundreds Of Germans, Italians and
japanese in Tampico, Veracruz
Tuxpan, Carmen and Progreso. II
follows a similar edict removing
their compatriots from vital Pacific
Coast zones.


All suspected of hostile activity
the immigration office said, will be
sent either to concentration camp
or to penal colony off the Pacific
Coast.


The new coastal cleanup was ini-
tiated soon after the arrest of nearly
so Nazi-Fascist agents, including the
reputed head Of the German Gestapo
in Mexico, who were interned in
Perote.


Fires and other damages in the
rich oil fields around Tampico in
recent weeks have stirred rumors
that Axis saboteurs were respon-
sible.

NEW BRUNSWICK, N. j., Dec.
19-Mrs. Frances Stevens Hall, the
aristocratic principal Of the Halls
Mills murder case, one of America s
most celebrated crimes, died today.
She was 70.


The murder 20 years ago of her
husband, the Rev Edward Wheeler
Hail. and Mrs. Eleanor Mills, at
tractive young choir singer in his
fashionable New Brunswick church,

The three were acquitted and

teries.


Many Angles to Case.


The case contained virtually every
element the morbid or the crime
connoisseur could desire.


The middle-aged rector and the
church sections wife were found
neatly laid out beneath a crab
apple tree on De Russey's lane, a
lovers trysting place.


The clergyman's calling card was
carefully placed against his heel:
the couples love letters were strewn
about the scene. The woman had
been shot three times and her
throat slashed; the clergyman had
been shot once.


The police inquiry got nowhere.


Four years later the case was
revived and Mrs. Hall, wealthy
granddaughter of one of George
Washington's aides, and the two
Stevens brothers went on trial


Public interest ran so high that
300 newspaper writer's and photo
graphers went to Somerville to re-
port the trial. They sent from
100000 to 100000 words of news
daily for the month it lasted.


Mrs. Hall, 18 years the senior of
her husband, denied all the charges

contention her husband was un-
faithful.


"Pig Woman" Testified.


There were 200 witnesses, but
none to compare with Mrs. Jane
Gibson, the Pig Woman" who made
dramatic appearance on her
death bed (she lived for four more
years. and in a graVelike voice testj-
fled from a hospital cot brought into
court past gaping spectators.


She was riding on her mule. Jenny,
down De Russey's lane the night of
the murder, she said, looking for
corn thieves when she heard shots
and saw Mrs. Hall kneeling over the
bodies.


Henry Stevens died in 1899. Willie
Stevens, the eccentric brother who
resided with his sister, is ailing and
spends most of his time puttering in
the garden instead of on the streets
or in fire houses, his favorite haunts
Henry Carpenter, their cousin who
was indicted but granted a sever
ance of trial, died in 1885. His in
dictment was quashed


James Mills, the church sexton.
lives. He never had much to say
since his wife left their drab home
the night of September IA. 1922,
and he asked where she was going


Follow me and find out" she

tenn.

representatives goods like food,
shelter material and other items.

United States with barrage balloons
for use on the Pacific Coast.

which this Government has been
signing with individual United Ma
tions governments since early in the
year provide for a reciprocal ar
rangement.

now being provided to us by other
United Nations without dollar pay
ment are machine tools, anti-air-
craft guns and ammunition, repairs
for vessels In foreign ports and air
rights for our air ferry services.

crop Of 1941.

average but still below last years
crop.

were reported light, with better
prospects for late fall and win
ter apples. Conditions were
slightly below average though,
Church said. Plums were also
below average.

emily referred to news from the

cipally in the dispatches of Swiss

country.

~MALL Russian Ludmilla sat on


the edge of the rye field, the
~ green meadow stretching be-
fore her. She had stolen out early,
and the sun had only just risen,
but already it was warming her, and
she was feeling sleepy.


Pleasantly half asleep, she now
saw something pretty happen. For a
while there had been a hunming in
the air, as of some music far away.
And now, far up in the sky, to the
left of the sun, big beautiful bubbles
were softly bursting into being one
by one. Slowly they were floating
down toward the earth, and she
thought she was dreaming. They
touched the horizon, and vanished.


But now there was another bub-
BILE, almost straight above her head.
1t came down swiftly, then slowly.
Now it looked like big mushroom.
And another mushroom, a baby one
this time was keeping it company.


Ludmilla drew back into the rye
and watched sharply out of her
hazelnut eyes. The little mushroom
landed, melted, and there stood a
big black box in the middle of the
meadow. The big mushroom landed
and stretched itself sidewise along
the ground, all fattened. And there
was man. He lay in the grass and
he had funny clothes and funny
hat. He lay on his stomach, his
face in the grass. and didn't move.


Ludmilla withdrew farther into
the rye, walked out sideways. and
ran toward home, back to Mother
and Grandfather. Even as she ran
she was remembering how nice her
grandfather had become ever since
her father had gone away. a sack of
food and a pair of extra boots on his
back.


He was the best grandfather now!

Brophy had reached this conclu-
sion after questioning $50 persons

vessel at the time of the fire.

Crimean Peninsula have put the
Black Sea area back on the active

Seminal results of the Argentine
congressional elections held on
March ! permit definite analysis
of the outcome in that important
political contest. The outstanding
features are the sharp contrast in
popular sentiment between BuenoS
Aires and the provinces, and a gen.
eral decline of the Radical party.


The first of these factors is nothing
new, because the great metropolis
on the banks of the Plate estuary
has always stood somewhat apart
from the rest of the country. 1t is
Argentina's one big urban center,
the provinces being predominantly
rural. Buenos Aires large working
class element tends to vote Socialist,
but outside the metropolis, which is
also the national capital, the Social
list party hardly exists. The two
nationwide parties are the Radicals,
representing chiefly the middle
classes, and the Concordancia, a
coalition of conservative elements
headed by the great landowners and
big business interests.


Acting President Castillo is Con-
cordancia's standard bearer, and the
recent elections were fought largely
on the issue of his foreign policy of
neutrality In the World War, which
the Conservatives strongly favored
while the Radicals advocated a break
with the Axis powers and whole
hearted Pan-American cooperation.
During the electoral campaign, Cas-
tillo strained his executive authority
to the limit by declaring a state of
emergency under which speech max
ing or editorials about the war were
forbidden. The consequence was the
curious spectacle of campaign con-
Quoted in silence on the burning issue
everybody was thinking about.


Early. returns from Buenos Aires
showed that the Conservatives were
faring badly. which led commen-
tatorS TO expect the Radicals would
increase their already strong repre-
sentation and control the next Con-
gress. But final results showed that
the big winners in the capital were
the Socialists, who headed the poll,
with the Radicals a close second and
the Conservatives bad third with
only one-fourth of the total vote.
The provinces went strongly Con-
servative, with the Radicals trailing
behind their showing in the previous
election. Apparently, the Radicals
will lose their plurality in the next
Congress to the Conservatives. Con-
cordancia, however, failed to get its
hoped-for majority. The Socialists
will hold the balance of power, and
they are expected to vote with the
Radicals on matters affecting foreign
policy, since they also are anti-Axis
and opposed to the governments
policy of strict neutrality.


Acting President Castillo thus pre-
sumably will continue to be faced with
congressional opposition. However,
it will not be as strong as in the pres
ent Congress. and the decline of the
Radical party undoubtedly will dis
appoint many observers in the United
States and other parts of Latin
America as well. CaStillo'S foreign
policy apparently has been indorsed
by the provinces, and the hold of the
Conservatives has been strengthened
over Argentine political life. What
this may portend for Argentina's
part in Pan-American affairs and its
attitude toward the United States
remains to be seen.

Competitive Hunger


1t is a sad commentary on our war;
blighted times that spring should be
the period in which food problems
become most acute. Under normal
peacetime conditions, our civilization
insures sufficiency throughout the
year. But wars voracious appetite
devours surpluses and brings on
chronic deficits. During the long
winter months, the warning countries
have been dipping constantly into
the carry-overs from last autumn's
harvests. BY spring, food reserves
have run low and must be carefully
stretched until the next {arvests,
still months away.


Even favored America, though
assured OF basic foodstuf1s, is having
lesson in scarcity by its impending
sugar ration, caused by large d.
versions 81 sugar stocks from human
consumption to war uses. Those
stocks cannot be built up until the
cane crops, foreign and domestic,
and expanded beet sugar harvests
this summer partly redress the
deficit. Our dietary shortages, how
ever are as nothing compared to
Europe's plight in its third consecu-
tive war spring. There, virtually
everything edible is short, and most
foods are either strictly rationed or
are entirely unobtainable.


The great war Of generation ago
taught that starvation is the most
terrible Of weapons. This grim les
son has been taken to heart; so,
from the very beginning of the pres
ent struggle, the war has been in one
aspect a remorseless duel Of COM
petitive hunger, waged respectively
by the British naval and German
U-boat blockades. Each recurrent
spring has seen belts drawn tighter,
and this season both sides appear to
be hard hit.


Britain as yet has escaped the most
severe consequences of blockade. No.
body goes chronically hungry, but the
drastically rationed diet is drab and
monotonous. Meat Is getting scarcer,
white bread is forbidden, eggs are an
exciting rarity, while luxuries Of all
kinds have disappeared. Conditions
are strikingly revealed by the growth
Of the so-called black market"
where the traditionally w-abiding
Briton breaks food-ration rules with
an ingenuity reminiscent Of our own
lawless practices under prohibition.


For the past two years Germany
has been staving of the British naval
blockade by Systematically plunder-
ing q conquered or browbeaten CONT
nent. But despite merciless lootings
which have reduced some countries
like Greece and Poland to mass
starvation, the Germans themselves
are going short this spring. Begin
ming April 6, basic rations of bread,
meat and fats In the Reich will be
drastically cut. And it should be
understood that those rations have
never been much above the subsist-
ence level. The German government
frankly warns its people that scant
relief can be expected from the con-
quered regions Of Russia, 50 thor
oughly "scorched" by the retreating
Reds last autumn. Thus the specter
Of hunger stalks across the conti-
nent, though the Germans presum-
ably will be the last to starve.


Both in Britain and on the CONT
nent, summer vegetables and fruits
will alleviate the crisis two or three
months hence. But harvest prospects
are none too good after q severe
winter and a three-year lack of
fertilizers for the hard-pressed soil.

fell out of the car, and Justice drove
the car some distance down the
road, then in rage turned it about

into the woods.

to the Senate; 10 v. Morgan, sole
member of the District Tax Appeals
Board; Col. j. H. Lewis, and Alex
ander Tucker, Department of Justice
attorney.

Col. Lewies had contended that
he could not become subject to the
Maryland income tax merely by
having residence in the State, be-
cause he had had no control over
orders commanding him to report
Tor Army duty in Washington.

While the Germans laid dowr

munity. Christian Education, Home

division would be enabled to main
tain direct relations with denomina-
tional boards and agencies CORE
spending to it's field of operation,
including those of denominations

ment OF commissions on missionary
education, stewardship, evangelism,
social industrial and race relations,
international justice and goodwill,
and education for service. The
Council also would operate service
bureaus in the fields of research.
publications, religious radio. church
building and architecture, and
publicity.

Bv Letfice Lee Street,


When Mary Jane saw her daddy's
car at the gate she dashed away
from her playmates, sped up the
walk and burst into the house,
the screen door banging loudly
behind her.


Hello, daddy" she called gayly
and threw herself upon him with
spontaneous delight.


Father frowned "How many
times" he asked, "have I told you
not to bang the screen door?"


"Oh, daddy" Mary Jane said
breathlessly, ignoring the remark;
"I have a real live turtle. Mrs.
Jones gave him to me and he has
roses painted on his back and he
is truly, really and truly alive! Do
you want to see him?" She was
dancing on tiptoes.


One braid had become loosened
during the vigorous activities OF
follow the leader" her socks were
wrinkled down into the heels OF
her sneakers, a jagged tear made
her gingham skirt sag to one side
But her smudgy, small face was
radiant with welcome.


Mother came into the room and
she froWned, too. Look at your
hair and your socks. Mary Jane!
And you've torn your dress"


Dresses cost money" added
father, still scowling.


At suppertime all that Mary Jane
heard was: Take your elbows OH
the table! Sit up straight! Don't
eat so fast! Don't talk with your
mouth full! No, you may not have
any more jam-no-no-no, don't,
don't, don't


If this father and mother, as
tired and worried as they may have
been that evening, could only have
forgotten their irritations long
enough to consider the effect OF
their words upon their little daugh-
ter their hearts would be sick.


Constant criticism. insulting dis
approval, black looks and words
cannot fail to wound child, make
her feel inferior and unloved and
cause a hurt, bewildered expression
to come into his eyes.


The light of warm welcome and
the shine of childhood happiness
does not have to be clouded In our
children's eyes. But we can only
keep the sparkle there by being
kind.


The next time you find you are
about to criticize your child stop
and think before you speak. Sharp
ness becomes such a nasty. insiduous
habit. Constant. useless criticism
has soured the romance OF many
a marriage and has broken the
peace of thousands of homes, leav-
ing wives, husbands and children
utterly miserable.


Remember that it seems as only
yesterday that your youngster was
a tiny baby, his head Graded on
your shoulder, now he is 7 or 4 or
IA. but whatever his age give him
time to learn and have patience
with his youthful mistakes.


Remember, too, that while you
may many times have a right to
criticize this act on your part does
not help matters, it only makes
them worse. Children respond and
learn much more quickly when
praised for honest effort and good
deeds than they do if they hear
only rebuffs and heart-breaking
criticism.

NEW YORK, Feb. 20.-The stock
market worked on starvation diet
today and, while numerous issues

strength, scattered motors, rails and
specialties managed to reach higher
ground.


Uneven tendencies prevailed at the

foggy at the close. Gains ranged

setbacks were in evidence.


Transfers of around 350,00O shares
were among the smallest since last
June.


Wall Street hunted unsuccessfully

in the war news and, with Japa-
nese thrusts continuing in the

position in the Philippines becom-
ing more hazardous, customers with
buying inclinations inclined to step
lightly. A little bidding here and

ern Union, American Can, General

Du Pont eventually revived.

BY the Associated Press:


SAN FRANCISCO, March s.
Alert seamen. who manned the
newly installed deck guns of the
big oil tanker William H. Berg,
today toasted a moral victory
over a Japanese submarine in
the first such exchange of shells
reported since the arming of
merchantmen began.


The underseas craft, presumably
Japanese, fired on the modern STAN
dard Oil Co. vessel without warning
late Saturday night. Unhit, the
tanker replied in kind. Deck guns
blazed away at the assailant, barely
visible in the darkness.


Whether the submarine was hit
was not known. Naval patrol
planes could find no trace of it
when they reached the scene.


Freighters and tankers, armed
and unarmed, have been sunk or
badly damaged by torpedoes before
their. crews could drop lifeboats or
aim cannon, but this was the f1rst
reported instance in which United
States merchantmen had fought
back and driven off the attacker.


The engagement, announced late
yesterday by the 18th Naval District,
occurred close to shore about 80 miles
below San Francisco. All radio
stations were ordered off the air
for half hour to prevent the enemy
from taking navigation bearings.


1t was the second attack by gun
fire in. California waters in five
DAYS. A big submarine shelled Oil
company property near Santa Bar
bara February % with scant damage
and no casualties. 1t was the first
raid on West Coast shipping since
last December, when underseas
craft attacked nine ships in six
days, sinking one and damaging
two.

Among the choicest of the berry,
bearing shrubs which are hardy in
protected places are the pyracan-
thas, or firethorns. Farther south
they make a magnificent show, and
they are conspicuous objects in any
favorable location.


Firethorns belong to the rose
family and are closely related to the
thorns and apples. Their fruit is a
small, brilliant-colored berry that
persists fairly we'll through the
winter. Even if you have to protect
them over winter, these shrubs are
worth growing.


Probably the hardest of the lot is
Pyracantha occinea, although sew
eral of the other species are fairly
hardy and have been grown extern
sively for decorative purposes. The
main thing is to keep the wood alive
so that the Towering buds which
were formed the year before are not
winter-killed. If you will do this
the shrubs are very profuse in their
development of small PONIES, or
apples, in the fall Of the year, and
persist until we'll after Christmas.


Pyracanthas are generally ever
green shrubs. They should have a
weI-drained location and one that
is protected from north and west
winds, but aside from this require
ment they are not particular as to
soil or other conditions. Not only
are these shrubs outstanding for
decoration around the house on the
outside. but they are very distinc-
tive indoors.

PORTLAND, Greg, May Ats
an eerie experience out here to
drive halfway up a snow-capped
mountain to look back down on the
Pacific Northwest's new DetroitS,
new Pittsburghs, new Birminghams.


Two years ago they were swamps,
COW pastures, apple orchards.


Today they are acres of concrete

mum for 10000 war planes a year,
rushing metal alloys for ships and
tanks, pouring out carbides and
CELEBRATES for explosives and phos-
phorus for incendiary bombs.


The plants are the birth of an

production.

centers today, this Northwest en-
pire has a chance to 60 on full
speed in peace.


Can Switch to Peacetime Work.


Except for the shipyards, the
plants here can switch to peace
time work: Phosphorus can be used
In fertilizers CELEBRATES in weed
killers and aluminium has a thou
sand uses.


It's an electrical empire far re-

the Northwest

up annexes out here as large as the
home plants. Daily, planes and

Portland Office of scholarly looking
DR.. Paul j. Raver, the administrator

&o"SA -NSA pOWSI.

No More Argument.


Bonneville and Coulee are the
huge Government-built dams on the
turbulent Columbia River. They
caused loud howls when they were
started early in the New Deal. They
were called "sociahstic," white ele-
phants" and "a tragic waste of the
taxpayers money"


Acknowledgements people pointed
out there was no market here for
more power, but their argument has
been drowned now in the war, The
power is needed.


1t was here, so the plants are
springing up on the high-lines from
the dams-even though the home
offices are 5000 miles away In New
York, Philadelphia and Baltimore.


The private power companies are
grinding out 100000 kilowatts
themselves. That might have been
enough for stagnant northwest
or even for a slowly growing one.


But now these companies are SELL
Ing every last kilowatt. And in ad-
dition, Bonneville-Co is ped
ding $4,000 kilowatts.


What's more, there's a waiting
list for Bonneville -Coulee power.
and some plants won't even be built
until next year because the power
isn't ready.


Generators Needed.

Congress must vote money for them.
And it's right there, in Capitol cor
ridors, that the fight still is raging.


BY the end of this year Bonne-
ville-Coulee will be grinding out
100000 kilowatts. If they get the
new generators they'll pour out
$4,000 kilowatts in 1943. For the
entire Nation the capacity is now
placed at about $4,000, 900 kilowatts.

Bonneville-Coulee system feeds five
huge aluminium plants, three i'm
mense shipyards and plants turn

INT and plant to fabricate alumni
mum.

tlonal Minerals and Chemical Corp,

SAN DIEGO, March 7.-On rolling
land between two valleys, half way
between Los Angeles and San Diego,
stands venerable Mission San Juan
Capistrano-the Jewel" Of Cali
fornia's mission chain.


Dedicated November /, 1776, Mis-
sion Capistrano has withstood time
and desecration to emerge one Of the
truly beautiful retreats of our West
ern land. To Capistrano's ivy cor
ridors, gardens and fountained
courts. come each st. Joseph's Day
March 49, the migrating swallows
long associated with the mission.
The birds nest under the caves of
the mission buildings throughout the
summer, departing, if no untoward
disturbances hasten them, on st.
Johns Day October 23,, the feast
day of the missions founder.


Mission Capistrano stands in the
heart of the California community
of that name but is curiousiy de-
tached from the scurrying traffic
which passes its gates. Tiny gates,
they are, opening into the world of
yesterday, when Spain governed the
sunny acres.


Passing through the tiny gates,
one finds himself in Capistrano S
famed Wer-garden-with foun-
tains and birds and ancient relics
intermingling. The incloSed area is
spacious. Vines and trails lead up to
and through the various ruins and
buildings. The mission buildings be-
speak the labor of expert craftsmen
The church, in partial ruins, COM
mands admiration. A cloistered
chapel with gold altar has been
faithfully restored. The Campanario
bells, hanging in time-worn adobe
walls, chime daily. The Indians of
Capistrano became skillful at weave
ing, tanning and masonry-ruins of
aqueducts, reservoirs, adobe walls,
arches and patios. denoting the skill
and energy applied in construction.


The Franciscans departed San
Juan Capistrano in 1888, by Mexican
order, and the missions decline fol-
lowed. For some decades. buildings
and grounds were neglected. Then
public-spirited citizens interested
themselves in the matter of restora-
ton.

the battle zone by five to one at the
outset of the offensive. During a
cold rain Saturday night the Ger
mans sent over heavy bombers flown
from Crete in an attempt to counter
the Allied bombirgs.


A communique from British head
quarters this morning placed heavy
emphasis on the aerial blows being
delivered against the enemy and
declared that Marshal Rommeps
attempts to close the gaps in his
lines had failed.


Enemy Attacks Repulsed.


"The enemy was unable to dis
close our troops from the areas
already gained" the bulletin said
laconically.


(The German high command


said the heaviest losses were
inflicted on the enemy during a


successful defense against the


British large-scale attack" One


hundred four British tanks were


declared destroyed.


(The Italians said British


attempt to land sea-borne troops


behind the Axis lines had failed


and declared all Allied frontal


assaults had been repulsed with


heavy losses.)


Axis air activity increased some
what yesterday as Rommel's flyers
sought to ward off the terrific bonn
$ bardment to which his ground
troops were being subjected, but
Allied pilots had a successful day,
shooting down seven enemy planes
and damaging many more, head
quarters declared. An Axis supply
ship also was reported bombed and
sunk in Tobruk harbor.


Minor Clashes Reported.


The communique mentioned only
minor clashes between armored
units, bearing out dispatches from
the front indicating that the main
armored strength of the opposing
armies was not yet engaged.


Marshal Rommel's armored for
nations, however, were said to be
moving up to meet the advancing
British forces, and it was these
units on which the full fury of the
Allied aerial assaults was concen-
trated.


American and British bombers,
flying in relays, dumped tons upon
tons of explosives on the massing
Axis armored division from dawn to
dusk yesterday, attempting to scat
ter and destroy them before they
could join the battle.


The attacks were pressed home
from low levels with strong fighter
protection and were almost unop-
posed, British headquarters said.


Official quarters gave few details |
yesterday on the progress of the
land fighting, limiting themselves
to the announcement that the enc !
my's main positions had been pene-
trated at some points, but there was
evidence of quiet confidence in the
outcome


Plans Well Laid.


1t. Gen. B. L. Montgomery, COM
mander of the 9th Army, said
plans for the offensive had been
well laid and that its objective was
to destroy Rommel and his army"


British and Allied troops fighting
in front are first-class soldiers and
I am determined they will have
success" he said.


While the full strength of the
forces massed by the Allies re-
mained military secret, it was
generally believed that they held
superiority in men, tanks, guns and
planes.


According to best estimates, Mar
shal Rommel has about 125,OOO men
at his disposal. These include two
German armored divisions, two Ital-
Ian armored divisions-the Trento |
and Folgoia; a German motorized
division; partially motorized Ger !
man infantry division, and at least
six Italian infantry divisions.


The Allied ground forces involved
IN the opening phase of the battle
were known to include Australians
and New Zealanders the 1st South |
African Division, the 4th Indian
Division, the 44th Home Counties
Division, TIE 50th Northumbrian
Division, the 5lst Highlands Division
and units composed of Fighting
French and Greeks.
No U. S. Ground Forces Engaged.


No American ground forces we're
engaged in the initial operations, but
the United States Army Air Forces
have been playing a major role.


A communique issued by United
States Army headquarters yester-
day said fighters, fighter bombers
and medium bombers of the desert |
air task force had made continuous
and repeated attacks on enemy
positions, gun emplacements and
motor vehicles.


Many direct hits were observed
on gun emplacements and motor
vehicles and many fires were start
ed the communique added.


Despite the extent of the Allied
aerial operations yesterday only -
planes were reported lost, and the
crews of some of these were saved. !
One Axis plane was downed-a dis
parity in losses apparently accounted
