If your perennial border has
rather moist but well drained soil,
partially shaded, and you'd like
some colorful, hardy plants for it
this year, try Trollius or globe
flowers. They produce snowy, long
lasting yellow and orange blooms
which resemble giant buttercups.


European globefower grows about
two feet in height and bears yellow
blooms. One of the best forms is
known as Giant Devonshire. There
are several other named varieties
but some of the handsomest kinds
are the natives of Northeast Asia.
namely Trollius chinensis, japonicus
and asiaticus. These bear yellow
and orange flowers that are very
handsome. One of the easiest of
this class to grow is Ledebouri which
bears beautiful yellow flowers in
early spring.


The globefowers generally bloom
in May or early June. They are
easy to grow if you give them
deep. fertile soil, around the neutral
point in reaction, and which doesn't
dry up during our hot summers.
They will persist for years in such
conditions.

BALTIMORE. April 6.-Harry

head on the pavement.

other man off O'Brien and he dis

unconscious, was sent to the hos

Inc war economy mas TaCeO across
America like a Kansas tornado, hit
ting here and skipping there with
no apparent reason.


Across America, towns bulgine
with war workers and booming with
war business sit beside towns full
of vacant homes and vacant shops


Both the boom town and the war
time ghost town are found in every
region. There are towns, too, that
are getting along'-no boom, nc
depression, just business as usual
The business has changed-the shoe
factory turns out Army boots, the
metal shop makes gun parts-but
the town goes along about the same


The boom is not limited to big
cities and the depression hits not
only in the small towns.


This is the overall picture seen in
confidential reports from Govern
ment field agents.


Big Centers Busting.


Hits: The big centers of bustling
business are pretty obvious-the
steel mill towns of the North and
the South. Detroit with its con-
verted automobile plants, Lower
California's aircraft centers, the
machine tool sections of Ohio and
the shipbuilding GEN.
ters along the coasts, the old Army
arsenal towns. With these go hun
dreds of small cities whose shops
were fit for conversion, whose loca-
ton was right for subcontracting


Less -obvious regional industries
have given a boost to business in
other places-the lumber industry
of the West Coast, with growing
backlog of untitled orders. Mime
sofas iron range, the copper mines
of Utah and Arizona, the chromite
and manganese centers in Califor-
mia, the centers of electrical manu-
facture in New York State and New
shoe towns and textile
towns adapted to filling orders for
the armed services.


Add to these the overnight bo-
nanzas where Army camps or naval
training centers have given business
a sudden push.


Despite the shortage of farm labor,
there is general agreement, too.
that towns which buy and sell from
the farms are mostly doing all
right. The farmers income has in
creased, and transportation bobbles
are forcing him to do more shopping
near home.


New York City Quiet.


Misses New York City, financial
capital of the Nation. is reported
There are few war in
dustries In Manhattan. The city's
argest industry-the 200, ,000-man
apparel-cutting and needle trade
has slowed up for lack of materials.
Foreign trade, life blood of the
great exporting and importing busi-
ness, has been cut to trickle. In
The merchandising centers, the out
look seems grim. The bulk of white
collar workers have not shared the
Dig pay increases of the wage earn
ers in factory towns.


Smoke -wreathed factories in New
Jersey, Connecticut and upstate New
York may take up some of the slack
in New York City's employment


The hard-coal mining region of
Pennsylvania, which lost many men
to the war industries around it, has
had its troubles, but the outlook is
not bad for the duration.


The distressed industries of the
South are the cast-iron pipe and
stove works and the silk hosiery in
dustry. For technical reasons, they
find it difficult to adapt their oper-
ations for war work.


Tourist Trade Hard Hit.


All along the Atlantic Seaboard,
of course, are industries suffering
from the transportation jam, caused
largely by the submarine marauding
on East Coast shipping. Chief
among these is the tourist trade.
which stretches along the coast
from Maine to Miami. The Army
and Navy have helped some of these
towns-dimmed out and quiet-by
training centers in their
once -swank hotels.


Other industries, too, have hit
the transportation snag-the sugar
refneries of the northeast, for in
stance, which used to get their raw
product direct from Cuba by boat.


In New England, they say: Sew
ing machines and stamping presses
are a dime Dozen"


In the Middle West, sluggish
areas often house factories built
for sheet metal work, metal stamp
ing. automotive trades, miscella-
neous wood products or gray-iron
foundries-industries which seem
likely workers but which are
equipped only for limited jobs in
the war drive.


Compared with the miners who
are digging the vital metals of
war-iron, copper, chromite, nickel
the gold miners of South Dakota
and the gold and silver miners of
the Far West consider their posi-
ton none too good. In the midst
of mining rush they are prac-
tically in the doldrums.


Wherever farmers till the soil the
promise of good prices is encourag-
ing, but the nightmare of good
crops without farm hands to gather
them is everpresent. Harvest days
will show how successfully this
shortage can be met.


That is the broad-brush picture.
Not every boom and bust of the
war is in it, but it gives you an
idea, perhaps, of the things that
wars necessities are doing to
America.

CHICAGO. June 15.-The war in
spired agricultural commodity price
rise and the almost uninterrupted
advance in wholesale food costs
since before Pearl Harbor have
definitely been halted, at least for
the time being, market statistics
showed today.


Although farm commodities are
exempt from blanket ceilings placed
on most processed food costs to con-
sumers, market prices now have re
treated from 1912 highs in the case
of all major products.


They are still we'll above year ago
levels, however, and experts said this
fact. coupled with greatly increased
wartime farm production, virtually
assures agriculture of near record
cash income this year. Preliminary
forecasts indicate marketings will
yield farmers about S2000,000, 900
more than the $l1,000,000,000 plus
income they received in 1941. Dur
ing the first quarter of 1912 cash
farm income was Al per cent greater
than year ago. Largest income on
record was ,60O,O00,0 900 in 1919;
the smallest since then, less than
S., ,000, 900, 900 in 1882.


Effects Differ.


Price ceilings as Of March highs
which went into effect last month on
most food costs in retail and whole
sale trade, directly or indirectly
affect farm commodities to varying
degrees, experts said. Some foods,
however, such as eggs and poultry
milk products, flour, mutton and
lamb, are exempt even in wholesale
and retail trade.


Various developments other than
price control have had important
influence in causing certain COM
modities to back down from 1912
highs, which, in most cases, were
tops for the past several years. For
example, excellent crop weather,
generally speaking, with near record
harvests in prospect and large car
ryover supplies on hand, have helped
to depress grains. Butter and eggs
have been affected by large supplies
coming to market as producers
swing into the greatly expanded war
production program. This is nor
mally the season for flush produc-

BY the Associated Press.


CAIRO, Nov. 21.-Striking swiftly
beyond wly-captured Bengasi, the
British 9th Army squeezed Marshal
Erwin Rommel's chastised Africa
Corps into the approaches of the
Ell Agheila defile tonight in a race
to deliver knockout to the hapless
Axis survivors before they could
burrow into the natural defenses
of that 3O-mile-wide Libyan coastal
strip.


British forward elements, now
more than half way to Tunisia from
their starting point at Ell Alamein
in Egypt, caught up with the Axis
rear guard at Agedabia, some 10
miles from Ell Agheila, yesterday.
With the 9th Army maintaining its
average advance of 80 miles day,
it appeared that the showdown clash
on the heretofore unbreached Ell
Agheila line was only matter of
hours away.


Marshal Rommel was believed al
ready to have gotten the main body
of his broken army into the Ell
Agheila area, which lies on the Gulf
of Sirte along the border between
Tripolitania and Cirenaica.


Perilous Position.


With most of his tanks gone and
with another opposing army behind
him in Tunisia, his position was a
perilous one despite Ell Agheila's
strong points. But in all probability
another major campaign with heavy
fighting will have to be fought be-
fore the Axis is driven out of Africa.


Regardless of what Marshal Rom
mel does now, his headlong fight
before the grimly pursuing British
has set record for backtracking in
more than two years of war in North
Africa.


The spectacular British drive has
pushed him back more than 600
miles as the plane flies and 800 miles
as the tank must travel from Ell
Alamein, where a month ago he
presented a mighty threat to Alex
andria and SueZ. That is more than
double the distance he forced the
British to withdraw last June.


Heavy Blows by Raj.


The Raj, meanwhile, was striking
heavily against Axis shipping in the
central Mediterranean in token of
what will come when Allied gains in
North Africa are turned into bases
for attacks on enemy communica-
tions and on the Continent itself


An 8,000-ton merchant vessel was
attacked off Cape Bon, in the Sicili-
an Straits, and another 1000 ton
ner sustained direct hits during an
attack by the Raj near Kuriet
Island off the Tunisian coast. The
latter was raked also by cannon
and machine-gun fire. These were
direct blows at efforts of the Axis
to establish itself across the straits
from Sicily in Tunisia.


Malta based British bombers at
tackled Catania, Augusta and Cosimo
airdromes in Sicily. Air-borne Axis
troops have been taking off for the
Tunisian front from these points.


The triumphant British entry into
Bengasi yesterday was the third in
this war and represented the fifth
time the Libyan port had changed
hands between the opposing forces.
Great Fires Blazing.


Gen. Sir Bernard L. Montgomery
men saw the awful results of the
continued pounding of the port by
British and American bombers be-
fore the Axis pulled out.


Moles, jetties and harbor installa-
tions were in shambles; great fires
still were blazing from the Allied
blows and from Marshal Rommel's S
own application of the torch.


One Raj pilot who got a close
view of the harbor said the scene
was one of almost unbelievable de-
struction and desolation." Smoke
still rose from wrecked ships dotting
the once-fine harbor.


American pilots flying four-mo-
tored Liberators played great part
in this vast blow to the enemy. For
months they bombed the port regu-

BY the Associated Press.


SAN JOSE, Costa RIGA, Noe. IA
Costa Rican coast guards were
credited today with driving of
German submarine which, an ON
cial announcement said, approached
the shore with the apparent inten-
ton of landing men to forage for
provisions or engage in sabotage.


The submarine was said to have
opened fire with deck guns when
spotted close inland at an unspeci-
fled point along the Atlantic coast,
but the craft sheered off and sub
merged when the fire was returned
from the shore.


Two members of the submarine
crew and Costa Rican coast
guardsmen were reported wounded
in the exchange. The announce
ment did not say when the Incl
dent occurred.


Costa Rica, bordering Panama on
the north, was the first American
nation to declare war on the Axis
after the Japanese attack on Pearl
Harbor, acting even before the
United States.

LONDON, Nov. 14.-Home-
based Raj Lancaster and Stir
ling bombers smashed anew last
night at Genoa, Italian supply
base for battered Axis forces in
North Africa, starting massive
fires which Rome acknowledged
wrought great destruction.


The giant British raiders, which
carry 2-ton "block busters" made
the hazardous 1,500-mile round
trip across the Alps without the loss
OF a single plane. 1t was the 10th
assault of the war on Genoa and
the fifth in less than a month.


"A cloudless sky was found over
the city and with the help of flares
targets were clearly identified" the
air ministry said. THE attack was
well concentrated and large fires
were left burning


Official Yugoslav quarters In Lon
don meanwhile quoted travellers
from Italy as saying the first four
raids in the last four weeks caused
damage aggregating $200,0O0,000 at
Genoa.


Heart of City Attacked.


Docks, warehouses and areas in
the heart of the city were reported
devastated by the massive British
explosives and showers OF fire bombs.


The italian high commands COM
munique today said the eastern and
central sections of the city bore the
brunt OF last nights attack.


Since the Germans have taken
over all France the Raj must fly
over enemy territory all the way,
unless short cut Is taken across
Switzerland. German fighters and
anti-aircraft, formerly encountered
only in Northern France, presum-
ably now are at Vichy and other
airdromes in the south.


A British informant said italian
defenses apparently were growing
weaker since no Raj planes we're
lost last night or in the October
% attack on Genoa.


With growing Allied air suprem-
acy in the Mediterranean, this
source said obviously Italy was due
for even heavier poundings from
Allied bases in Malta, Libya and
shortly in Tunisia.


Second Blow In Week.


1t was the second blow in q week
at Genoa. The Raj smashed at
Genoa in successive raids Friday and
Saturday of last week to cripple
the warehouses and transportation
facilities serving the German Italian
desert troops of Marshal Erwin
Rommel.


Air raid warnings sounded in
Bern, Geneva and Lausanne last
night as they have on previous
occasions when Raj planes were
striking across the Alps. The alerts
lasted from 10 to 81 minutes.
The night sweep followed a day
In which Allied fighters carried out
offensive patrols over Nazi-occupied
Holland and Brittany.


Canal barges and railway loco
motives were attacked" the Air
Ministry said. "None OF our aircraft
is missing"

BY the Associated Press.


LONDON, Dec. Lord Linlith-
gov will remain Viceroy of India for
an indeterminate period because
Prime Minister Churchill has been
unable to find suitable successor,
the News Chronicle said today.


Linlithgow's five-year term ex-
pired in April, 1941.


Sir Archibald Sinclair, secretary
of state for air, turned down the
post, the newspaper said, and then
Viscount Cranborne, lord privy seal,
was considered, but he is in poor
health.


Others believed to be under con-
sideration, the News Chronicle
added, are Clement Attlee, secretary
of state for dominion affairs; Lord
Halifax, Ambassador to the United
States, and the Duke of Devonshire,
parliamentary secretary for the
India office.

Rochester.


He pleaded self-defense because
Lockwood advanced threateningly

yard to demand that Lockwood
leave Mrs. Crenshaw alone.

It's a chancey business, this
grape picking job in the High
Sierra. For mont h s we've
watched the green and purple
clusters ripen-maybe.


Sometimes a late spring frost
wipes out all our hopes, leaves
the vines barren.


Sometimes an early autumn
freeze or storm destroys the
harvest. Always there are anx-
ious days, watching the sun
and wind and rain. Getting up
at night to check the thermom-
eter. Wondering if the vineyards
will win through.


This year they've won. Dawn
after dawn has flooded like an
amber tide.


The leaves sprawl bronze and
crimson on the reddish earth.


The oaks are turning rust and
scarlet and maroon. The dark
blue mountain jays squawl nols-
lily.


Close TO the gnarled gray
trunks, the muscats CLEAN in
crisp and emerald globes, all
honey sweet


Beside them. Zinfandel and
missions cluster, smoky, violet,
their .odor musky as their drip
ping juice. The warm air fer
ments with their heady wine.


Men Start Picking


Down the long lanes and vines
the empty Tugs are space q.
stained with the fragments dye
of many years. With the slow
dawn, the dew evaporates.


The men are waiting for the
mist TO lift. They smoke and
talk. Then. when the haze has
changed from blue TO rose. they
90 10 work, III cir long. slim
bodies bending to the waiting
grapes.


Their brown hands clasp the
vines. The fragrance breaks
across the morning air. The slow
sweat spreads across their faded
shirts. The pink dust rises from
their Flooding feet, their bend
ing knees.


We're Fighting For


/ look and listen-and / think.


These are the things our boys
are fighting for.


In Egypt, England and Aus
tralia, the Aleutian Islands, in
China, Russia and the Solomons.
these are the things our boys
are fighting for. For things like
these, we pour blood and wing
our faith.


Nor for fine words we cannot


understand,


But for the dear and homely


things OF earth
For Jugs of grapes,
For folds of narrowed soil.
For fiocks OF sheep.

Heavy Jungle Encountered.


Armchair strategists should see

tain roads over which supplies must

men themselves plough through mud

itous mountain tracks which even

ing equipment

indicate whether the Allied forces

pass to the northeastern slope of

however, that the threat to Port
Moresby had been smashed for the

The enemy, as We expected, has
discovered his supply problems, ag-
| gravated by constant air attacks,
were impossible of immediate solu-
| ton"

| statements.

vainly to keep supplies flowing
through the Owen Stanley Noun.
tains to their forward positions.

more than 300 miles from New

and taken to Buna much in tn.

During the passage and attel

little food and no medical attention

bayonet point to work day and nigh

Many Of the natives died and, sur

ward along the tracks, pushing tn,

The National Music Council has
just completed survey of the num-

port that they have no women play
ers, although the Cincinnati SYM

The largest number of women mu-
sicians are in the Pittsburgh SYM
phony, which has seven such musi-
clans playing violin, viola, cello and

Francisco Orchestra has five women

and narp desks. TWO Of these have

The National Symphony and the

and celeste. The four women play
ers in the National Symphony in
clude violinist, cellist, oboist and
harpisE. The harpist has been with
the organization for nine years, the
violinist and cellist four years each,
while the oboist has had one year Of
service with the orchestra.


The Philadelphia Orchestra has
woman violinist, cellist and harpist,
who have seen seven years, six years
and one years service, respectively.
The Philadelphia Orchestra has had
other women harpists for many sea-
sons, however. Two women play in
the Detroit Symphony, a violinist of
three years service and harpist Of
five.


Six orchestras have only one wom-
an player each, the Chicago. Cleve-
land, Kansas City, Los Angeles,
Rochester and st. Louis Symphonies.
The Chicago Symphony has a wom-
an horn player who has been with
the organization for one year, and
the Los Angeles has had woman
violinist for four years. The women
players in the other four orchestras
of this group are all harpists, and
they have been with these orchestras
for long periods, varying from 8 to IL
years.
1t is evident from the survey that
during the season of 1912 there
was no great necessity for replacing
drafted men players with women
musicians. This picture, however,
may be drastically altered during the
coming season.

ron. said the shelling was accurate
and perfectly timed, catching the
Italians completely by surprise.


The island is in the extreme East
ern Mediterranean close to Turkey,
and is the largest of the Dode-
canese.


Tells of Seeing Fires.


AS the squadron steamed away,

Mr.. Nixon said

miral P. l.. Wan, carried out the
bombardment with the accuracy and
perfect timing of a postman deliver
ing the morning mail.


The British warships entered
enemy waters and approached the
target without being detected before
they opened fire.


Planes Aid in Action.


Reuters said planes co-operated In
the action, dropping flares, spotting
targets for the ships, and bombing
the airdrome simultaneously with
the sea attack.


Despite efforts of Italian shore
batteries and the presence of E.
boats, all our ships and aircraft re-
turned without scratch the Reu-
tiers correspondent wrote. Cooper
alton between sea and air forces was

Atlantic City's gosl.

ing fleets with lateen sails,

There lay the bay.

hate

For in that moment hate was


wiped away

And suddenly I saw a little OF


The Plan

man.
saw that God draws close as

that I was here

SINGAPORE, Jan. 81. The
"Johnnies" are in Johore. They are
ready to defend Singapore as they
have defended all Malaga from the
northerpmost battlefront to where
the Japanese, reinforced by sea and
land, are now attempting to force
a line of invasion southwark.


Who are the Johnnies? The john
MES are Gurkhas, partly Mongol by
origin and the least known heroes
of this heartbreaking battle for the
richest province in British posses
sion. The Johnnies come from the
high jungles of Nepal. north of
India. When the Australians went
into action some II days ago, they
went into the headlines, too.


But nobody has heard much about
the Gurkhas for the simple reason
that nobody could get to where they
were.


Beyond impossible rivers and sag
ging, exploded bridges after the last
motor trucks have retreated south
ward; beyond the airdromes with
their craterlike holes to occupy Jap
engineers; far beyond the point
where correspondents can go. were
the Gurkhas-holding. delaying
sniping, ambushing, saving the lives
of retreating comrades.


Bombed necessarily.


The Gurkhas have been continu-
ously rearguarding down the entire
$50 miles OF that bloody north-south
highway through the Malayan Pen
insula. They have been subjected to
literally incessant bombing and ma
ne-gunning for more than six
weeks.


What we have been through
surpasses Norway. Dunkirk and
Greece" said one British officer to
your correspondent. 1--WE began
north of Alorstar, December 8, and
this is the first rest we've had.
Please remember, our boys are little
more than II and l8 years old and
they've been facing seasoned troops.
Six months ago many Of them had
never seen lorry, a machine gun or
an artillery piece, to say nothing OF
Jap tank"


Against the young Gurkhas the
Japs turned loose their tanks from
the beginning. A heavy Jap tank
was met at Ultra, north OF Alorstar-
proof conclusive that Thailland was
cooperating as a military base with
the Japs long before the hostilities
began. The technique employed
here by the Japs was to send
heavy tank in advance, with three
lighter tanks following. The large
bulk and heavier armor Of the first
tank was intended to protect the
others. Here a sergeant major met
the onslaught with an anti-tank
gun which put the leader out. The
Japs later developed a variant OF
this attack, using heavy tank
equipped with a cannon but also
mortar. Lobbing shells 300 yards in
advance, the mortar was intended
to dispose of the anti-tank guns.


Most Terrible Encounter.


The most terrible encounter by
the Gurkhas with tanks occurred
at the Slim River. The Gurkhas'
British officers, many of whom were
newly arrived from England and un-
able to speak Gurkhali, had estab-
ished headquarters at point slight
ly south from the river, where the
embattled north-south highway
makes a hairpin loop. Camp was
pitched in a rubber grove, midway IN
the loop.

usual intermittent machine cunning

They'll be coming soon." He meant

rattling sound coming down the
road. III


Must be Bren gun carriers" said

quarters.


Deploying themselves along the

guns around to aim through the
scattered rubber trees. Their move
ments were leisurely. They even
called out 'banzai!" (hurrah) to the
trapped Gurkha leaders and took
time to hand out the Rising Sun
flag.


Rubber Grove No Cover.

wards. and their shells were 3.5's.

withdrew Monday and the Allies
recovered their original positions.


German panzer units were

killed in the final round of the day
long battle"

mans wounded and taken captive

through with fighting.

Sammy Jay had spread a false re-
port all through the snow-covered
Green Forest and over the glisten-
ing Green Meadows. He had told
every one he met that Farmer
Browns boy had killed poor Mrs.
Grouse and taken her home for his
dinner. Now, it was true that he
had taken her home, but it wasn't
true that he had killed her. You
see, he had found her very weak
and helpless under the hard, icy
crust that Jack Frost had made
while she was asleep down under
the snow, and which she couldn't
break. Sammy Jay and Peter Raf-
bit had both seen her carried away
and both knew that she hadn't
been killed. But it made a bigger
story, a more dreadful story, to say
that she had been killed, and
Sammy Jay dearly loves to tell bad
news. Besides, he is always ready
to think evil of others.


IF he didn't kill her, then he will
kill her when he gets her home"
said Sammy to himself, land SO it's
all right to say that he has killed
her" So he flew about spreading
that dreadful false story and actu-
ally enjoyed telling the dreadful
news.


Of course, all of the friends Of
Mrs. Grouse felt terribly. Some
of them Peter Rabbit saw and he
told them Sammy jays story was
not true-that Mrs. Grouse had not
been killed. But he had to admit
that she had been carried away by
Farmer Browns boy, and to her
friends this seemed almost as bad,
for most of them were very much
afraid of Farmer Browns boy and
quite willing to believe the very
worst of him. So they all mourned
for poor Mrs. Grouse and said how
dreadful it was and how they hoped
that some day something dreadful
would happen to Farmer Browns
boy.


But Mrs. Grouse didn't know any
thing about this. At first she had
been terribly frightened when she
had been picked up and knew that
Farmer Browns boy held her a
prisoner. But after q while his
hands felt warm, for she was shiv-
ering with cold, and they seemed
very gentle. And then. she didn't
know why, she wasn't afraid any
more She just cuddled right down
and felt sure that nothing dreadful
was going to happen.


And nothing dreadful did happen
Oh, my, no! She was taken up to
Farmer Browns house and right
inside, where it was as warm as in
summer and where Farmer Browns
boys mother stroked her with such
gentle hands and said, You poor,
poor little bird" And then when
she was warm she was taken out
to the henhouse and put In a box
with plenty Of nice warm hay and
there she was left with all the corn
and oats and barley that she could
eat. This was what she needed
most, for you know it was because
she had had nothing to eat for so
long, while she was a prisoner under
that dreadful icy crust, that she
was too weak to fly when the crust
was broken.


So she ate and ate until she could
eat no more and then nestled down
in the soft, warm hay to sleep, for
she was tired. so very, very tired.
And as she closed her eyes it seemed
to her that she couldn't remember
when she had been so comfortable
certainly not for days and days.
And she could sleep without fear
of Reddy Fox or Hooty the Owl or
any other danger. To be sure she
was a prisoner. but somehow she
didn't mind. Not then, anyway.
And-and-well, Farmer Browns boy
wasn't dreadful at all: he was rather
nice.

ceeds and buys still more feed to

ture.

CHUNGKING, May 23.-The
Japanese have occupied Chuan-
Shih Island at the mouth of the
Min River below Foochow, in
Fukien Province, after the
Chinese once chased them back
to their ships and wiped out
more than half their landing
force, the Chinese announced
tonight.


The Japanese thus increased their
threat to all China's eastern sea-
board while contending armies were
locked in a bloody struggle along
45-mile front in Chekiang Prov
ince, adjoining Fukien on the north.


The landing on Chuanshih was
made Wednesday under cover of an
intense naval and aerial lombard
ment after part of some $4,000
japanese troops attacking the
Fukien coast under protection of
10 warships had been repulsed.


The same day the Chinese re-
pulsed another attempt to put
troops ashore on Pingtan Island,
less than 20 miles to the south.


Planes Bomb F0Ochow.


The communique said 81 warships
were shelling this island and Nam
jisii Island to the south and that
planes bombed Foochow and Mamoi,
Min River port on the mainland,
just across from Chuanshih.


In Chekiang. on an arc extending
from the north to the east of
Kinhwa. the japanese scored a 35-
mile advance with their right wing
and were hammering hard with
their left.


Advancing from Tunelu. on the
north side of the Chientang River
IS miles southwest OF Hangchow,
the japanese were approaching
Kienteh, about 80 miles north of
Kinhwa, with the support of bomb
ing planes which attacked the de-
Tending forces in relays all day.


This column obviously was aiming
at Lanchi, on the south side of the
river and only IL miles northwest of
the provincial capital.


Northeast OF Kinhwa, at Pukiang.
Yiwu and Tungyang, triangle of
towns which form the outer defense
line of the provincial capital, the
Japanese were definitely slowed
down with the Chinese hurting back
assault after assault


1000 Reported Killed.


Two thousand Japanese were re-
ported killed in sanguinary battle
north of Yiwu, 80 miles northeast of
Kinhwa, but the invaders were
rushing up assistance. CThe Japa-
nese claimed they had stormed into
Yiwu.)


Tungyang was besieged.


The far southwestern front facing
Burma was comparatively dormant,

further success in driving the Japa-

Big See-Saw Struggle.

hint of some German progress was

battle in the main as a stupenduous

Such wedges as the Germans

RICHMOND, Va, June 20.-Many
of Virginian's picturesque and beau-
tiful scenic possessions by the sea,
in the mountains, beside lakes and
rivers and in forests and rolling
inland have been included In the
State park system.


There are three mountain parks.
Douthat, near Clifton Forge and
Hungry Mother. near Marion. are
in the rugged Allegheny Mountains,
while Fairy Stone, near Bassett, Is
at the foothills of the Blue Ridge.
Seashore Park is on the Chesapeake
Bay, near Cape Henry; Staunton
River Park is in the rolling Pied
mont section near South Boston, and
Westmoreland Park is along the
Potomac River, near MontroSs.


First opened in 1886, these rec
reational areas have been steadily
improved and provide ideal places
for men, women and children to
spend short or extended vacations.


There are 81 housekeeping cabins
throughout the system, these being
fully equipped and furnished. They
rent for a minimum period of one
week or for a maximum period OF
two weeks. Westmoreland Park has
six low rental cabins, having only
for overnight or weekend guests.


Douthat and Hungry Mother
Parks each has a guest lodge, fully
equipped and furnished, for over
night or weekend visitors. Each
park provides water sports, picnic
areas with shelters, trails and bath
house service. Each has restaur-
ant and store from which prepared
meals, groceries and other provisions
may be obtained.


Three parks, Westmoreland, Hun
cry Mother and Fairy Stone, have
modern tent and trailer camping
areas with such modern convent
ences as tested drinking water. a
central washroom with laundry,
showers and sanitary facilities, elec-
trio plug-ins for trailers, submerged
garbage disposal cans and outdoor
cooking ovens with fuel provided
without cost. Hungry Mother Park S
camping area will accommodate Is
trailers and an equal number of
tent camps; Fairy Stone, IL trailers
and 13 tent camps. and Westmore-
land, II trailers and 13 tent camps.


Virginia's State parks are operated
by the Virginia Conservation Com
mission, Division of Parks, Rich
mond.

CIFIC, Dec. 6 Delayed Two sea-
men who risked their lives and a
destroyer captain who risked his
ship to save survivors from a car
rier sunk in the battle of Santa
Cruz Island October 26 were cited
for heroism today.


Admiral William F. Halsey, fleet
commander in the Southern Pacific,
made the awards aboard a ship
at sea. The Navy Cross was given
to Comdr. Wallis Frederick Peter
son, Council Bluffs. Iowa and Silver
Stars to Torpedoman First Glass;
James A. Golden and Seaman (First
Class o. S. Downie, both of Vine
yard Haven, Mass.


Additionally, the Navy Cross and
Distinguished Service Medal were
presented to Comdr. Arnold Ellis
worth True of San Carlos, Calf =,
and Corinth, KY. He was the cap
tain of a destroyer which rescued
survivors of the carrier Lexington
in the battle of the Coral sea and
later was sunk trying to save the
carrier Yorktown off Midway.


L was a lucky witness to the feats
for which Comdr. Peterson. Tor
pedoman Golden and Seaman
Downie were honored but had not
met the men until today.


Came Alongside Carrier.

screen the carrier was on dts loss

against relentless attacks by Jap
bomber and torpedo planes.

brought the destroyer alongside by
superb seamanship. Disregarding
the imminent danger of further
aerial attack. the little ship pumped
water and helped extinguish fires
aboard the carrier


Although three times driven of
as the Japs repeated their bomb
ing and torpedoing, Comdr. Peter
son each time returned alongside
and took survivors aboard. This
continued until every survivor had
been picked up by his and other
ships in the task force.


Torpedoman Golden and Seaman
Downie, both of the same destroyer,

ence during three and half hours

safety, he courageously braved the
shark infested waters to assist in
the rescue of survivors. Once he
swan without life vest to the aid

Torpedoman Golden also made re-
peated trips with lines and buoys to

ice Medal was in recognition Of

NEW YORK, May 28.-At last
the shadows of war are closing in
ON New York. There's grim and
brooding atmosphere about the. big
town these nights.


The streets are becoming dimly-
lighted canyons. The towering
buildings loom dark against the soft
May skies with only occasional blobs
of lighted windows to sharpen their
outline The crowds seem subdued
by what has happened TO their once
brilliant playground.


But with all the dim-out that
has robbed the city of its garish,
colorful, sparkling glare, the shad-
oWs must become even deeper to
remove the sky-glow from millions
of lights which might silhouette
ships at sea.


Maj, Gen. T. A. Terry, command
ing the I'd Corps Area, said the city's
glow was still "murderous mound
Of light" endangering the ships of
the United Nations.


Night Spots Are Crowded.


Authorities are considering a
blackout OF advertising signs for the
duration and further dimming of
street lamps.


Tourists who come to New York
for their summer vacations are going
to find the city has changed its
nighttime appearance since they
last saw it.


The Gay White Way? It's still
gay enough behind the blackout
curtains. The night spots and bars
and dime-a-dance halls are crowded


The headlines no longer chase
each other across the front OF the
Times Building. The huge Wrigley
sign has come down. Theater
marques no longer blaze the names
of stars. Flashing signs studded
with thousands of bulbs have been
switched off.


Street Lights Shaded.


Crowds wander through Times
Square in a dusk-like glow contrast
ing strangely with the glare that
flooded this thoroughfare only a
few weeks ago


Even the street lambs are shaded
with black band of paint to keep
the light from shining upward.


Travellers returning from Europe
accustomed to stumbling through
blacked-out streets-once gasped in
surprise at Gotham's glitter. But
no more. The shawl of protective
darkness is being pulled tighter from
the penthouses to the Bowery.


With transportation difficulties
growing, the flow of tourists into
New York probably will be cut
sharply this summer-but on the
other hand, more New Workers will
stay at home.

of the most significant psychological

World War II.


These prospective heroes are the bonn
bardiers who will man the famous Amer

transcend anything yet seen. All OF them

will be personally blasting place for

enemy target while hostile fighters zoom
out of the clouds.

terials to finish their jobs. The out

dence offered against any one de-
fendant might cast shadow on all

conspiracy charged and that no rea-
sonable grounds existed for sever
ances. He dismissed the petition
without hearing arguments.

Britain suffered two grave re-

With the collapse Of British re-

causeway to the mainland and called

Burma is the gateway 10 the vast

bulletin regarding the Moulmein

casualties had been inflicted on the
Japanese.


The Salween flows from the north
and empties into the Gulf of Mar
taban at Moulmein, 100 miles east

has been mentioned as the possible
first line for a British defense stand
in Burma. Military experts said po-
sitions behind the Salween will be
much harded for the Japanese to
crack than Moulmein.

fluid"

munique said Moulmein was under

out yesterday, with British defense
forces communicating In an ef-
fort to halt the Japanese.

said to have been directed against
Martaban. just across the Salween
from Moulmein.


Moulmein itself was bombed, and
Rangoon had two alarms although
no planes were seen over the city.


Japanese accounts of the attack
on Moulmein said the city had been
left virtually deserted and that its
approaches were heavily mined. A
Domei broadcast from Toxic indi-
Gated the principal attack on the
city came from the southeast, where
the Japanese crossed the Ataran
River in small boats. The Ataran
and the Salween Rivers join at the
eastern outskirts of Moulmein.

still alive.

tracks. One tank car in the freight
train burst into flames.

ANNAPOLIS, Sept. 10.-Comdr.
Arthur J. White, hero of the ILL
fated aircraft carrier Lexington.
received the Navy Cross yesterday
in simple ceremonies at the Naval
Academy.


One of the Lexington's senior
medical officers, Comdr. White was
cited for his refusal to abandon ship
although both his ankles and a
shoulder were fractured and nu-
merous wounds were inflicted by
two explosions which shattered the
carrier in the Coral Sea.


While Japanese torpedo planes
and dive bombers dumped their
loads on and about the Lexington.
the doctor, native of West Leipsic.
Ohio, transferred his wounded and
dying patients from a shattered
dressing station and thence to
rescue ship before leaving his post.


Comdr. White first was wounded
when a blast all but DESTROYED the
dressing station he directed. Covered
with blood and hobbling about with
fractured ankles, White transferred
all his patients to another impro-
vised station, but then had to aban-
don these quarters when the second
blast came.


Although the carrier was burning.
Comdr. White would not quit his
post until his final patient was re-
moved.


The medal was presented by Rear
Admiral John R. Beardall, Naval
Academy superintendent, acting for
Navy Secretary Knox on behalf of
President Roosevelt.

Weekly busting with a soft

made with the smallest amount

direction until the dirt has been
dislodged. Then rinse away the
soap with a sponge squeezed out
in clear warm water.


Dry the woodwork with
clean cloth. This sort of regu-
lar care will not only keep the
baseboards attractive but will
also make frequent repainting
unnecessary.

Tne belated announcement OF the
loss of four heavy cruisers-three
American and one Australian-dur-
ing the early stages of the Solomons
attack brings to light what probably
is the most costly engagement in
which any American naval squadron
has participated.


In its original announcement of
this battle, fought during the night
of August SO, the Navy listed our
casualties as "at least one cruiser
sunk and two cruisers, two destroy
ers and one transport damaged"
The latest report reveals that the
United States cruisers Quincy, Vim
cennes and Astoria, as well as the
Australian cruiser Canberra, whose
loss was announced some time ago,
were sent to the bottom. This in
formation, the Navy says, was with
held for security reasons until new
ship dispositions could be made. In
other words, the original announce
ment was intended to mislead the
enemy concerning the extent of the
damage he had done. If, Incl
dentally, the American people also
we're nnisled, it must be assumed that
the necessity of protecting the men
remaining in the Solomons area was
sufficient justification.


The latest story of the fight itself
conceals nothing of the extent of the
disaster. Piecing together the official
communique and the reports of sur
vivors, it seems clear that the Amer
lean squadron was surprised. The
Japanese opened fire at exceedingly
close range and the American ships
were heavily hit before they could go
into action. The Quincy and the
Vincennes went down during the
night, and the Canberra and the
Astoria sank the following morning.
Happily, a majority of the crew men,
bers we're saved, but the Navy states
that the loss of life was heavy. Ap-
parently the enemy squadron escaped
without ship losses, although it
seems probable that some of their
vessels were damaged.


There is consolation to be derived
from the fact that the American
cruisers, while paying with their lives,
were able to keep the enemy from the
troop transports, which was their
primary mission. They fought gal
lantly and to the end. But there
should be no attempt to minimize the
daring, the skill and the marksman-
ship of the Japanese. Their triumph
was a notable one, and it should
dispel the last doubt that we are
faced with the toughest kind of a.

mond contended before the court

standing.

Deal, for the new Congress will

Progressive

QUARTERS, Australia. Sept. 30.
Allied mountain troops, Sitting
through the difficult jungle and
mountain country of the Owen
Stanley Range, have captured
the first objective of their New
Guinea offensive, sent the Japa-
nese into hurried northward
retreat and seized quantities of
abandoned Japanese equipment,
communique said today.


Consolidating their positions on
IoribaiWa Ridge, which was retaken
from the enemy, the Allied troops
are pursuing the japanese toward
Nauro, 10 miles north of the ridge.
where the Japanese have Established
new defense positions.


With the conquest of Ioribaiwa
Ridge, which the Japanese had pre-
pared for defense with barricades
and field trenches, the Allies have
successfully started the difficult and
perilous task of driving the enemy
back over the 88-mile trail to Buna
along which he advanced to threaten
the Allied advance base at Port
Moresby.


Strong Resistance Expected.


Our advance continues" Gen.
Douglas MacArthur's communique
said.


1t was expected that strong re-
siStance would be encountered near
Nauro village and the creek at the
base of the next mountain ridge
north of IoribaiWa.


The fact that the Japanese aban-
doned many supplies, military
spokesman said, could not be taken
as an indication they were in rout.


Flank attacks by Australian troops
presumably forced the japanese to
leave precipitately without chance
of wrestling equipment and supplies
over the difficult terrain, he said


Allied bombers pursued the re-
treating Japanese relentlessly,
pounding their rear positions at
Menari. 4 miles north of Nauro.

At the same time heavy bombers
moved down the trail to Buna and
destroyed six barges used to trans
port supplies down the coast Other
enemy installations on the beach
and airdrome also were attacked.

Salamaua, large japanese base up
the New Guinea coast from Buna.
bombing the airf1eld and dispersal
areas. Results of the attack could

said

determined because of the rugged

village of Ioribalwa, as we'll as the
ridge, was taken.


The Japanese radio broadcast
report last night that japanese
naval units had made landings in
the Tanimbar. Kei. Aru and Babar
Islands between Australia and New
Guinea.


For some time it has been con-
ceded that the key points in these
islands were in Japanese hands and
Allied communicates have men,
toned attacks on Japanese Ship
ping around the islands of Tanim-
bar and Kei.
